_doc: THE BACKLOG. Every finding this project has ratified and not yet resolved, with a state and an owner. Prose in a report is not a record: three parties identified the divergent-repeat defect and it was ratified twice before an operator tripped over it, because nothing converted a ratified finding into a tracked one. Silence is not a valid state here.

_states.OPEN: Acknowledged, owned, not fixed. A valid resting state. The suite does NOT fail for OPEN findings, because a permanently red suite is a muted suite and this project has watched that happen three times. What the suite refuses is a finding with no state, no owner or no closes_when.
_states.FIXED: Resolved. Must name fixed_in. If it carries a check, that check becomes a REGRESSION test and the suite fails if it stops passing.
_states.WONTFIX: Deliberately not fixing. Must carry a reason.
_states.REVERSED: The finding itself was false. Must carry a reason naming who reversed it and on what evidence. Distinct from WONTFIX, which is a decision not to act on something real, and from FIXED, which would leave the record claiming a defect existed.

_closes_when_check: The generalisation of the mechanism that already worked once. An expectedFailure tracking `units` flipped to an unexpected success the moment the fix landed and held the suite red until the record was updated. Here: a check on an OPEN finding that PASSES fails the suite, because the finding is already fixed and the record is lying. A check on a FIXED finding that FAILS also fails the suite, because the fix regressed.

findings.title: Digest canonicalisation is not published
findings.summary: Two conforming implementations compute different digests for the same units because the contract never says how to canonicalise. The reference uses sorted keys, compact separators and ensure_ascii defaults; nothing publishes that.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states the canonicalisation exactly, and an implementation following only the contract produces the reference digest for a non-ASCII payload.
findings.note: Published as ordered steps plus four test vectors the code is checked against, so the contract and the implementation cannot drift silently. [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] CORRECTION TO THE TRIAGE. Both arms found canonicalisation unspecified, but they read the contract pinned at 378d641, which PREDATES this finding's fix in nxb-024: the pinned file contains no occurrence of canonical, utf-8, sort_keys, separators or nfc. So their agreement is NOT evidence that this gap is currently reachable; it is evidence about a superseded contract. The pin lagged HEAD by two commits and 28 percent of the file. See BLIND-10 for what IS still open in the current text.

findings.title: Exit-code convention is unwritten
findings.summary: The reference maps OBSERVED/REFUSED/UNKNOWN to 0/3/4, deliberately avoiding 1 so a naive shell check cannot merge REFUSED with UNKNOWN. The contract says nothing, so another implementation may use 1.
findings.closes_when: contract.json binds process exit codes to return states.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] NOT REACHED BY EITHER ARM. Zero hits for exit code, exit status or exit-code across both raw streams. CAVEAT: the brief asked for an implementation, not a CLI, so neither arm built a process boundary and this may be unreachable by construction rather than undiscoverable. Weak evidence, recorded as such.

findings.title: What produces state UNKNOWN is unwritten
findings.summary: UNKNOWN is in the enum with no clause saying what causes it. The reference has never emitted one.
findings.closes_when: contract.json names the conditions that produce UNKNOWN.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by BOTH arms, independently, from the contract alone. Neither had been told.

findings.title: Whether a REFUSED return carries pending_ref is unwritten
findings.summary: The reference returns it for post-receipt refusals; the blind arm does not. Both are contract-compliant.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states whether pending_ref is present on REFUSED.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by Arm A, which raised the receipt-versus-pending_ref distinction unprompted.

findings.title: reason is not bound to the refusal vocabulary
findings.summary: The reference appends a colon and free-text detail; the blind arm emits a bare vocabulary term. Nothing says which is right, so no consumer can parse reason safely.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states whether reason is a bare term, and where detail goes.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] NOT REACHED BY EITHER ARM. Both read the refusal vocabulary, neither raised that `reason` is not bound to it. This one WAS reachable: both arms invented refusal reasons while the published vocabulary sat in the same file, and neither noticed the two were unconnected.

findings.title: last_proven_at is inert and how it is ever set is unwritten
findings.summary: The field is required, never read since the freshness budget was deleted, and nothing says what would set it.
findings.closes_when: Either the contract says what sets it, or the field is removed.
findings.note: Worker 1 is researching whether the liveness claim should be deleted entirely. DO NOT PRE-EMPT. [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by BOTH arms, which each invented a LIVE value and a setter for a liveness state machine the contract never defines. The doc phrases this as the liveness state machine rather than as last_proven_at, but it is this finding.

findings.title: Dedup versus validation order is unwritten
findings.summary: Both implementations check the dispatch key before validating the envelope, by coincidence rather than by clause. The order is observable: it decides whether a malformed repeat is a dedup hit or a validation refusal.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states the order.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by Arm B: an envelope naming an unregistered runtime is malformed_envelope under one reading and runtime_unregistered under another. Arm A did not reach it. [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by Arm B, which also derived the observable consequence: because the receipt is persisted BEFORE validation, a rejected envelope still returns state OBSERVED. That is what the unwritten order actually produces, and it is recorded here rather than as its own finding because it is this finding's effect.

findings.title: dispatch_key when it cannot be extracted is unwritten
findings.summary: dispatch_return.dispatch_key is required, but a malformed envelope may have no key to echo. The reference emits an empty string.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states what dispatch_key holds when the envelope has none.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by BOTH arms; both independently hit the dispatch_key empty-string fallback.

findings.title: The bounded return budget is prose with no number
findings.summary: The spec states a MUST that a dispatch call always returns within a bounded budget. The contract carries no timeout and nothing enforces it.
findings.closes_when: Either a budget is published and enforced, or the MUST is withdrawn.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] NOT REACHED BY EITHER ARM. One incidental mention of budget in Arm A, no finding from either. Reachable in principle from the text; nobody looked.

findings.title: The reference's canonical form is not always valid JSON
findings.summary: Canonicalisation can emit a form that is not valid JSON, so a digest is computed over bytes no conforming parser accepts.
findings.closes_when: Canonicalisation emits valid JSON for every input the corpus contains, proven by round-tripping every corpus entry.

findings.title: The reference digests text it cannot transmit
findings.summary: An unpaired surrogate is digested but cannot be encoded for transport, so the guarded value and the delivered value can differ.
findings.closes_when: Either such input is refused at the boundary, or the digest is taken over the transmittable encoding.
findings.note: Fixed alongside N-1: both are 'digesting something that cannot survive the wire'. Refused with uncanonicalisable_payload rather than settled by an encoder flag.

findings.title: Unbounded, deadline-defeating WRITE path
findings.summary: The read path was made non-blocking three times; the WRITE path was never audited. The adapter streams every byte a child emits into events.jsonl with no cap and no deadline, so a chatty or hostile child can defeat the budget and fill the disk. This is the fourth instance of the blocking class and it subsumes the uncapped-events item I reported separately in nxb-014.
findings.closes_when: The write path is bounded in bytes and cannot extend past the caller's deadline.
findings.note: The write path is capped at 8MiB and emits a truncation marker, and is behind the interrupting deadline so a blocked write cannot outlive the budget.

findings.title: A peer can make the broker burn a core for the whole budget
findings.summary: A child that keeps a pipe readable without completing a line spins the select loop at ~98% CPU for the full budget.
findings.closes_when: The loop cannot exceed a bounded CPU share regardless of what the child does.
findings.note: Measured 61% of a core before, 0% after, on a child that closes stdout and keeps running. The deadline also held at 4.01s against 4s where it had overshot to 6.23s.

findings.title: _kill can raise, and the raise escapes its handler
findings.summary: The kill path catches OSError but other exceptions escape, so the refusal that F-15 promises can itself fail loudly in a caller that was promised it never raises.
findings.closes_when: _kill cannot raise; every failure becomes a recorded refusal.
findings.note: Fixed opportunistically while rewriting the kill path for the deadline work. Was not in the dispatched eight.

findings.title: The 5s start timeout is under-justified as an extrapolation
findings.summary: Measured warm max 0.167s and one cold sample at 0.685s. 5s is 30x the warm max but rests on n=7, one machine, one prompt size, a warm cache and a good network.
findings.closes_when: Either a wider measurement supports the number, or the number is derived per-runtime from observation rather than chosen.
findings.owner: orchestrator: needs a decision on whether to measure wider or derive per-runtime

findings.title: thread.started proves local startup, not capability
findings.summary: The start signal fires before any model work, so it proves a process launched and a thread was created, not that the runtime can do anything. F-1's registration gate rests on it.
findings.closes_when: Either the liveness claim is narrowed to what the signal proves, or a deeper signal is found.
findings.note: Worker 1 is researching whether the liveness claim should be deleted entirely. DO NOT PRE-EMPT.

findings.title: The live child is the only state not correlated to a receipt
findings.summary: last_handle is a single unkeyed attribute on the spawn hop, so concurrent spawns would collide and a handle cannot be traced to its receipt.
findings.closes_when: Every live child is keyed by its parent receipt id.

findings.title: events.jsonl is silently corrupted at 64KiB boundaries
findings.summary: Buffered writes split at buffer boundaries produce truncated lines in the recorded stream.
findings.closes_when: The recorded event stream is byte-faithful, or its corruption is detectable.

findings.title: Spawned children are not process-group isolated
findings.summary: A spawned child shares the broker's process group, so signals intended for one reach the other and a child's own children survive a kill of the child.
findings.closes_when: A spawned child runs in its own session and process group, and a kill reaps its descendants.
findings.note: Two fixes, and the first alone did not work. start_new_session isolated the group but the grandchild STILL survived, because a non-interactive shell sets SIGINT to IGNORE for background jobs, so the polite signal killed the leader and left its children. And the pgid must be captured WHILE THE CHILD LIVES: after the leader is reaped os.getpgid raises, so a group resolved at kill time is exactly the group you can no longer find. The self-kill guard is load-bearing: if start_new_session ever failed to take effect, a killpg would reap the broker and every sibling, so _own_group refuses to signal a group we are inside.

findings.title: A changed payload under a repeated key returned the old receipt
findings.summary: State OBSERVED, exit 0, the original receipt and the digest of the OLD units, so an operator believed a correction had shipped when it had not.
findings.closes_when: A repeat whose envelope differs is refused.
findings.note: [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by Arm A, stated as 'the contract only says what a repeat does, never what a repeat-with-different-payload does'. NOTE THE ASYMMETRY: the CODE was fixed in nxb-021 and the CONTRACT still does not say, so a fresh implementer reproduces the original hole. A code fix did not close the contract gap and this finding reads as FIXED.

findings.title: Retrying a refused dispatch converted it into a success
findings.summary: Same envelope twice: REFUSED then OBSERVED. Pressing up-arrow laundered a refusal.
findings.closes_when: An identical repeat replays the original disposition.

findings.title: Idempotency was silently scoped to the current directory
findings.summary: The default ledger was hidden, gitignored and cwd-relative, so two shells disagreed about whether work had happened.
findings.closes_when: A relative ledger path is refused and the resolved path is echoed.

findings.title: The alarm could not fire on the surface an operator had
findings.summary: PARTLY FALSE AS RELAYED. What is true: Ledger.undisposed() is structurally always empty on the H1-only path, because H1 records a disposition synchronously, and the CLI had no command to reach any alarm. What is false: undisposed() was never the alarm. Outbox.pending() was, and it existed and could fire.
findings.closes_when: The firing alarm is reachable and reports a count.
findings.note: Kept FIXED because the actions taken were right for reasons other than the ones given: the always-empty function was deleted and the real alarm was exposed on the CLI. Recorded here because a fix that lands correctly from a wrong premise is the kind of thing that reads as confirmation later.

findings.title: The CLI raises where the API promises never to
findings.summary: Passing an envelope as inline JSON, the natural first guess, produces a raw traceback with internal paths and echoes the whole payload back as a filename. A list-shaped registry also tracebacks. Neither says what the argument should be.
findings.closes_when: Every CLI argument error is a message naming what was expected, never a traceback.
findings.note: NEVER RELAYED. The cold pass reported seven findings; four reached me.

findings.title: pending() and peek were not on the public surface
findings.summary: The briefed interface did not exist where an operator would look.
findings.closes_when: The alarm and collect are reachable from the CLI.
findings.reason: FALSE FINDING, reversed by the worker who raised it and verified independently at nxb-026: pending() and peek() both existed at 977252a, nxb/h4.py lines 84 and 91, plus RoundTrip.pending() at nxb/roundtrip.py line 103. The cause was a scoped search reported as an unscoped conclusion: a hardcoded seven-module introspection list that omitted the two modules containing the functions. The CLI exposure done in nxb-021 was still a real improvement, but it was not a fix, because nothing was broken.

findings.title: The implementation emits an observer token the contract no longer uses
findings.summary: Every receipt carries a hardcoded observer value; the contract example was neutralised in nxb-016. Operator-visible divergence between code and contract.
findings.closes_when: The emitted observer matches what the contract publishes, or the contract says the value is free.
findings.note: NEVER RELAYED.

findings.title: units was hashed, counted, guarded and never delivered
findings.summary: F-8 and F-9 guarded a decoy while the payload that reached the worker was unguarded.
findings.closes_when: units is the payload the runtime receives.

findings.title: The declared start_timeout was ignored
findings.summary: A runtime declaring 30 silently got 5.
findings.closes_when: The declared start_timeout is read from the capability declaration.

findings.title: evidence_for walks the whole session tree on a miss
findings.summary: Unbounded work over a directory the runtime never prunes. 304 files and 1ms today; it grows for the life of the machine.
findings.closes_when: The walk is bounded, or the lookup is indexed.

findings.title: An H3 receipt is addressed to a dead sender
findings.summary: The four-hop model requires every hop to emit a receipt to its sender. H3's sender is a one-shot child, gone before its report is read, so the rule is vacuous there. The model assumed all four hops have living endpoints in both directions.
findings.closes_when: The model states which hops have a living sender, or the rule is narrowed.

findings.title: capability_declaration presents as configuration and functions as a comment
findings.summary: Ten fields of which three are read. This project's founding defect recurring inside the thing built to fix it.
findings.closes_when: Every mandatory declaration field is either read by code or documented as declarative in the contract itself.

findings.title: The never-read guard has four named evasions
findings.summary: Variable keys, getattr and kwargs splatting are invisible; it scans only the package; its guard-function list is by name; and delivered_wholesale is an unverified claim.
findings.closes_when: Either the evasions are closed, or each is accepted in writing.

findings.title: No transactionality between the state store and the filesystem
findings.summary: Receipts make an inconsistency visible; they do not prevent it. A receipt without a task folder is an alarm, but the write is not atomic.
findings.closes_when: The two writes are atomic, or divergence is detected and repaired.

findings.title: Hand-delivery has no receipt and cannot be instrumented
findings.summary: A receipt-less transport can be labelled or banned, not measured.
findings.closes_when: Hand-delivery is either forbidden or carries a manual receipt.

findings.title: A sandbox refusal narrated as done is undetectable, and how far that reaches is PER-RUNTIME
findings.summary:
Reworded on Rohan's ruling after nxb-029 measured a second runtime. This was stated as a universal property of brokering; it is not. It is per-runtime and it has two tiers.

HARNESS-MEDIATED DENIAL, where the runtime's own permission layer refuses a call: CLOSED for Claude Code's spawned-child path. It emits system/permission_denied mid-stream plus a structured result.permission_denials, and it SURVIVES NARRATION, measured across 3 runs and 2 tools where the model's entire output was 'DONE' and the denial was recorded anyway. OPEN for Codex, which emits nothing.

SANDBOX REFUSAL, where the runtime PERMITS the call and the OS refuses the effect: OPEN ON BOTH RUNTIMES. This is the original shape and no runtime measured here reports it as a refusal. Claude Code still beats Codex: the failed call is structurally visible as a tool_result with is_error true and a non-zero exit, which the model does not author, where the full 6-frame Codex trace contains no event for the denied write at all.

The distinction in one line: 'Claude Code has a refusal signal' and 'Claude Code can detect a sandbox refusal narrated as done' are different claims and only the first is true.
findings.closes_when: Closes only when the SANDBOX tier is covered: a runtime reports an OS-level refusal of an effect inside a call it permitted, or every dispatched task carries an externally checkable effect. The harness-mediated tier being closed on one runtime does NOT close this, and this finding is deliberately not split into a fixed half and an open half, because the distinction is the whole value of the record.
findings.note:
RULED BY ROHAN, relayed via Orchestrator 2: reword as per-runtime, keep OPEN. He was offered and DECLINED two other options: a standing rule routing risky work to Claude Code, and closing WONTFIX. No routing rule exists and none should be added, and nothing here refuses based on which runtime is dispatched to.

EVIDENCE: evidence/nxb-029/, 11 runs, raw frames. Also evidence/nxb-002-codex/sandbox-denial-invisible.jsonl for the Codex side.

THE TRAP AN IMPLEMENTER WILL TRIP OVER: result.is_error is false and subtype is 'success' in ALL ten nxb-029 runs, including every one with a denial. Neither is a work-was-done signal. The denial is only ever in permission_denials, in the permission_denied frame, or in the tool_result. Machine-readable scope per declaration is in _refusal_scope; see nxb/h3.py REFUSAL_SCOPE.

findings.title: Stale session identity is dropped silently on the PEER path
findings.summary: A /clear rotates the session id while ref, pid, socket and name stay intact, and a send carrying a cached id is dropped with no signal, so a sender caching identity at dispatch time goes 0-for-N against every worker cleared since. MEASURED on Claude Code's PEER-MESSAGING path in nxb-001.
findings.closes_when: EITHER peer messaging is built and re-resolves identity immediately before every send, OR the decision not to build it is recorded. Both close it; a decision is as valid a closure as code, because the alternative is a finding nobody can act on.
findings.owner: Rohan: a scope decision, not an engineering task
findings.note:
BLOCKER CORRECTED, nxb-037. It previously said 'blocked on a Claude Code adapter that does not exist', written by me in nxb-024. THAT WAS WRONG IN A WAY THAT COST AN ORCHESTRATOR REAL TIME: the adapter now exists, so the note read as unblocked, and it is not. The adapter is SPAWN-shaped and reads session_id off the child's own init frame, caching nothing, so it cannot exhibit this defect at all. W3-10 is about PEER MESSAGING, and there is no peer-messaging code in the tree. Search behind that claim: no send path exists in nxb/; the only sender is the spawn adapter, which never caches an id.

SO IT WAS NOT MISDESCRIBED, IT WAS MISFILED. It is not a defect in this system; it is a CONSTRAINT ON A PRODUCT THAT DOES NOT EXIST, and one I argued in nxb-031 is a separate product rather than a later phase of this one. Recording it as an engineering backlog item made it look like work someone could pick up, which is what nearly happened twice. Re-owned to Rohan as the scope decision it actually is, with a closes_when a DECISION can satisfy.

findings.title: Provenance is asserted, never authenticated
findings.summary: Anything local that can write to the peer socket is received as a trusted peer. The contract records this as enforced_by NOTHING, declared open.
findings.closes_when: Either sender identity is authenticated, or every consumer is told attribution is asserted.
findings.note: NOT CLOSABLE BY ME. Authenticating a sender is the permission boundary, which Rohan owns and I am instructed not to design. [BLIND ARMS nxb-041] REPRODUCED BLIND by Arm B, which raised dispatcher_id as unauthenticated from the contract alone.

findings.title: Pattern-based process cleanup reaps other tenants
findings.summary: Closed inside the package by an AST test; nothing prevents a future adapter or script from shelling out to a pattern kill. It has already destroyed another worker's run once.
findings.closes_when: No process is killed except by a handle its killer owns, enforced beyond this package.

findings.title: Cost instrumentation was deleted and not replaced
findings.summary: The only token-cost measurement in the project was removed when the canary collapsed into the round trip. The recommendation to return it as a provenance field on every dispatch was adopted and never dispatched.
findings.closes_when: Token cost is recorded in outcome provenance on every dispatch.

findings.title: Truncation is undetectable on a byte-lossy transport
findings.summary: The digest guard closes truncation only where bytes are preserved. On a transport that reformats, no honest sender-side digest exists.
findings.closes_when: Byte-lossy transports are refused, or carry their own integrity signal.

findings.title: The blocking class is ended by an interrupter, not by a fifth audit
findings.summary: Four instances of one wrong pattern: a deadline enforced by checking the clock between operations, so any operation that does not return makes the deadline unreachable. Each was fixed as an instance.
findings.closes_when: Every budget in the adapter is enforced by something that can interrupt a blocked operation from outside it, so a blocking call is survivable rather than fatal.
findings.note: Deadline fires a breaker from a timer thread; for a child the breaker kills it, which EOFs the pipes and unblocks reads and breaks writes. This does not make blocking calls correct, it makes them non-lethal, which is the property each of the four instance fixes provided for one call site only.

findings.title: The finding ledger could not record that a finding was false
findings.summary: States were OPEN, FIXED and WONTFIX. A reversed finding fits none: FIXED claims a defect existed, WONTFIX claims a real thing was deprioritised. The first reversal in the project had nowhere honest to go.
findings.closes_when: The ledger has a state meaning the finding itself was wrong, requiring a reason.
findings.note: Found by the mechanism meeting its first reversal, not by review.

findings.title: The negative signal cannot fire on a slow outage, because nothing is announced
findings.summary: nxb/failsignal.py consumes the runtime's own failure announcement, which collapses a connection-refused outage from 28.9s to 7.2s. Measured against a SLOW outage instead, an endpoint that accepts the TCP connection and then never answers, Codex emits no error frame at all: the connection succeeded, so there is nothing for it to announce, and the abort can never fire. Over 6 runs the outcome is bimodal: 3 hit the canary deadline at 25.5-25.6s with the generic reason no_output_file, and 3 were caught at 5.0s by F-15's start_timeout because thread.started never escaped before the hang. So the bound is start_timeout in half the runs and the canary deadline in the other half, and which one you get is not controlled by anything.
findings.closes_when: A slow outage, an endpoint that accepts and does not answer, is detected by something other than a deadline expiring, and the reason names the condition rather than no_output_file.
findings.note: Measured over 6 runs, not reasoned: per-invocation -c provider injection pointed at a local socket that accepts and holds, never a config edit. The person who measured nxb-022 predicted this case and asked that it be tested rather than assumed. It was tested, and it is not covered.

findings.title: CANARY_DEADLINE_S is set from one sample, not a distribution
findings.summary: nxb/canary.py sets CANARY_DEADLINE_S = 30.0, roughly 8x the single measured healthy canary round trip of 3.5s (evidence/nxb-022/timeline.json). One sample is not a distribution. This project has twice found that machinery justified by an unmeasured constant gets widened until it stops firing, and nxb/h4.py refused to add a delivery timer for exactly this reason.
findings.closes_when: A distribution of healthy canary round-trip times exists across both runtimes and the deadline is set from its tail, or the deadline is removed because something else bounds the canary.
findings.note: Mitigated but not resolved by the same change: because the runtime's announcement is now consumed, this deadline is the BACKSTOP rather than the detector in the announced case, so a wrong value costs a slower abort rather than a missed failure. FAILSIGNAL-SLOW is the case where it is still the only thing bounding the canary, which is why it is not closed.

findings.title: A closes_when_check that greps source is coupled to file layout
findings.summary: Two FIXED findings reported as regressed when nxb-027 moved the spawn and drain loops into a shared base. Nothing regressed: the checks grepped a named module, so they were testing where the code lived rather than whether the property held. A false regression is the mirror of the false green the ledger exists to prevent, and it trains a reader to disbelieve the ledger.
findings.closes_when: Checks assert the property behaviourally, or search for it without naming a module, so relocating code does not read as losing a property.
findings.note: Found by the ledger firing on its own author during a refactor. The two checks are now behavioural: one instantiates the bounded writer and writes past its cap, the other proves the deadline's breaker fires while the caller is blocked.

findings.title: refusal_signal_available() is a boolean over a tiered reality and now overstates
findings.summary: nxb/h3.py:161 refusal_signal_available() returns declaration.get('refusal_signal') is not None, and records it in every outcome's provenance. nxb-029 measured that claude_code's refusal signal is real but SCOPED: harness-mediated denials produce a system/permission_denied event and a structured result.permission_denials entry, while an OS or sandbox refusal inside a PERMITTED tool produces neither. Setting the declaration non-null flips this function to True, so provenance will now assert that claude_code can report refusals, without the qualifier that it cannot report the sandbox-shaped ones W3-9 is about.
findings.closes_when: Provenance records the SCOPE of a runtime's refusal signal rather than a boolean, or the boolean is renamed to say what it actually means, so no consumer can read 'can report refusals' as covering sandbox denials.
findings.note: Flagged by the worker who made the change that caused it. The declaration edit was the task; this consequence was not, and shipping it silently would have made the broker claim more than the measurement supports. FIXED in nxb-033: the boolean is gone. nxb/h3.py:refusal_scope returns a sorted list from the closed REFUSAL_SCOPE vocabulary, provenance records refusal_scope, and the overstatement never existed in a landed commit because the declaration's refusal_signal was set in the same change that removed the boolean.

findings.title: Frames buffered in spawn were discarded at the handover to drain
findings.summary: spawn breaks out of its read loop on the start signal, then drain built a NEW line reader, so any frame already split off, or any byte already buffered, was lost with the discarded reader. A child emitting its start frame and its result frame in ONE write lost the result entirely and the turn read as never having completed. LATENT IN THE CODEX PATH SINCE nxb-010 and never observed there because a real model turn puts seconds between the two frames.
findings.closes_when: The reader is handed from spawn to drain and un-consumed lines survive a consumer that breaks out of the loop.
findings.note: Found by the named 'read the code after the happy path passes, and ask who writes the state this depends on' step, not by a test. The state was handle['result_frame'], written only by _note_terminal, which only drain calls.

findings.title: --json-schema takes the schema inline, not a path
findings.summary: Codex's --output-schema takes a PATH. Claude Code's --json-schema takes the schema ITSELF. Passing a path makes the child exit 1 with 'not valid JSON: JSON Parse error: Unexpected identifier'. The dispatch described the flag as the direct analogue of Codex's, which is true of purpose and false of calling convention, and an adapter written from that description does not work.
findings.closes_when: build_command inlines the schema read from the path the shared interface passes.
findings.note: Reported to the orchestrator as a finding about the dispatch, in the terms it asked for: a flag existing in --help is not a flag working, and the analogy held for the wrong half.

findings.title: No registrable Claude Code declaration existed for a spawned child
findings.summary: Both declarations described the peer-messaging path. without_broker_inbox has a null start_signal so F-1 refuses it; with_broker_inbox describes a socket the spawn path does not use. A child the broker starts needs no inbox: its start signal is on its own stdout.
findings.closes_when: A spawned_child declaration exists, registers under F-1 and F-2, and carries a start_timeout derived from measurement.

findings.title: A refusal signal for Claude Code: unmeasured by me, measured by nxb-029
findings.summary: I observed permission_denials PRESENT AND EMPTY in a result frame on a run with nothing denied, and filed it as a candidate. While I was working, nxb-029 measured something better and different: a dedicated mid-stream `system/permission_denied` event carrying tool_name and tool_use_id, which their note says SURVIVES NARRATION. SOURCE: nxb-029's in-flight, uncommitted edit to contract/runtimes/claude_code.json and docs/REFUSAL-SIGNAL-nxb-029.md. I have not verified it and do not assert it.
findings.closes_when: nxb-029's measurement is landed and ratified, and the spawned_child declaration's refusal_signal is promoted from null to the measured event with its evidence path, by whoever verified it.
findings.note: If it holds, this runtime is the FIRST in the project with a non-null refusal_signal and W3-9 stops being universal, which is a bigger result than this task. My spawned_child declaration still says null on purpose: asserting a peer's unlanded measurement as my own is the founding defect wearing a friendlier face. CLOSED by nxb-033, by the worker who measured it. spawned_child.refusal_signal is now the measured event with its evidence path and its scope. Your instinct to leave it null rather than assert a peer's unlanded measurement was right, and the null outlived the measurement by exactly one commit.

findings.title: --permission-mode manual is accepted by the CLI and does not take effect
findings.summary: Claude Code CLI 2.1.251 lists 'manual' among --permission-mode's choices and accepts it without error. Measured [nxb-029 e2_manual]: the tool was ALLOWED, no denial occurred, and the system/init frame reported permissionMode 'default' rather than 'manual'. By contrast --permission-mode dontAsk IS reflected, init reads 'dontAsk', so init does report the mode faithfully when the mode takes. Anyone constraining a spawned child with 'manual' believes it is constrained and it is not.
findings.closes_when: Either the flag takes effect, or the broker never passes it and instead verifies the mode it asked for against the permissionMode reported in system/init before trusting any constraint.
findings.note: UNVERIFIED whether 'manual' is silently normalised to default or ignored outright; only the observable is measured, which is that what you asked for is not what you got. The general defence is cheap and does not depend on the cause: init reports the mode, so compare it to what you passed.

findings.title: A verified measurement was written onto two declarations it was not taken on
findings.summary: nxb-029 measured refusal_signal and terminal_signal on the SPAWNED-CHILD path, claude -p with --output-format stream-json, where the broker reads the child's own stdout. It then wrote both onto without_broker_inbox and with_broker_inbox, which are SendMessage peer transports that never hand the broker that stream. Two genuine UNMEASURED nulls were overwritten with a measurement from a different transport, and the one declaration the measurement did belong to kept refusal_signal null.
findings.closes_when: A declaration's signal fields state the transport they were measured on, and a measurement is landed against the declaration whose transport it was taken on.
findings.note: Caught by the author, in the next task, while reading the file for a different reason. Worth recording for the verification lesson rather than the mistake: the evidence was checked hard by two parties. Orchestrator 2 re-parsed all ten jsonl files, confirmed frame counts, narration survival at n=2 and the absence of false positives. All of that was true and none of it could catch the error, because verifying that a measurement is CORRECT does not check that it is attached to the right SUBJECT.

findings.title: A retry destroyed the answer it was retrying to obtain
findings.summary: RoundTrip.dispatch did not know H1 had deduped, so it re-entered the pipeline; spawn_once correctly refused the duplicate, and RoundTrip recorded that refusal as a fresh RUNTIME_FAILED outcome, OVERWRITING a delivered report. R-051 exists so a retry after an UNKNOWN is safe, and instead the retry was the most destructive action a caller could take.
findings.closes_when: A replay returns the stored outcome, and only after H1 has had the chance to refuse a divergent envelope.
findings.note: MY FIRST FIX REINTRODUCED F1. Short-circuiting to the outbox before H1 meant a changed directive under a reused key silently returned the old answer with exit 0, which is the exact defect a cold user found in nxb-019. Caught by testing the property rather than the fix. Ordering is the whole of the correct answer: H1 refuses divergence, then the outbox answers.

findings.title: F3's refusal was unreachable from the CLI
findings.summary: Ledger refuses a relative path. Every CLI command called os.path.abspath first, so it always handed over an absolute one and THE REFUSAL COULD NEVER FIRE. Measured: `nxb pending --ledger rel/l.db` created ./rel/ and reported success. The defect F3 was written to prevent, idempotency silently scoped to your current directory, was fully alive on the only surface an operator uses, from nxb-021 until now.
findings.closes_when: A relative --ledger is refused rather than resolved, at the CLI and in run().
findings.note: Same family as C14 and the never-read guard: a check that exists and cannot fire. Found because a test I wrote for a NEW command failed, and the failure turned out to be about the old ones.

findings.title: run_canary discarded clear_disproof's return value
findings.summary: clear_disproof returns False when the proof fails verification. The canary ignored it, so it could report ok True while its own proof was rejected and a standing disproof survived. Treated as a bug rather than a choice, because it contradicts the rule applied four lines earlier in the same function, that an unprovable pass is not a proof.
findings.closes_when: A canary whose proof fails verification fails, and records a disproof.

findings.title: Nothing used nxb, including the people building it
findings.summary: RoundTrip was the only code that spawns a runtime and returns an answer, and its sole caller in the tree was the canary with a hardcoded trivial payload. The CLI offered no command that returns an answer. Every real dispatch, including the ones commissioning this work, went over SendMessage as prose with no receipt, ledger, retry safety or alarm.
findings.closes_when: One shell command takes a directive and a runtime and returns the worker's answer, doing H1 through H4 underneath.
findings.note: `python3 -m nxb run --runtime claude_code --ledger <abs> --directive <text|@file|->`. Verified against a real child: F(12) came back 144 in 8s with a receipt, a ledger row and provenance.

findings.title: work_dir was accepted, threaded through, and consumed by nobody
findings.summary: Popen had no cwd=, Codex spent work_dir on -C, and the Claude Code adapter took it in build_command's signature and never read it. So a dispatched Claude Code child ran in THE BROKER'S OWN SOURCE TREE with Edit, Write and Bash: a worker dispatched by nxb could modify nxb, including the adapter that spawned it and the ledger recording it. Three real children read git status, git log and HANDOFF.md, honestly, while looking for a directive.
findings.closes_when: The shared base sets cwd=work_dir, so ignoring it is not expressible by any present or future adapter.
findings.note: Found by Orchestrator 2 reading the run ARTEFACTS, not the code: the system/init frame reports cwd. THE NEVER-READ GUARD DID NOT CATCH IT because the guard checks contract FIELDS and this was a function ARGUMENT. That blind spot is a bigger finding than the bug and belongs to whoever owns that instrument. Evidence preserved at evidence/nxb-031/work-dir-defect.json.

findings.title: What a spawned child is HANDED is undeclared, and only a denylist removes it
findings.summary: A spawned Claude Code child gets 31 tools including Bash, Write, Edit, Task, SendMessage, Workflow, CronCreate, RemoteTrigger and WebFetch, plus three connected MCP servers (Gmail, Drive, Calendar). The capability declaration describes how a runtime SIGNALS and says nothing about what it is GRANTED. Measured levers are in evidence/nxb-031/levers.json.
findings.closes_when: EITHER Rohan re-rules once the condition changes, OR the declaration records the grant alongside the signals. THE CONDITION IS THE TRIGGER: the moment anything outside this repo dispatches through nxb, or nxb runs anywhere other than Rohan's own machine, or a child is dispatched with a directive Rohan did not author, this ruling has expired and MUST be put to him again before that dispatch happens. Do not treat the existing ruling as covering it.
findings.note: MEASUREMENT ONLY, no recommendation, per the standing rule that Rohan designs the permission boundary. The two numbers that matter: --restricted removes 5 of 10 dangerous tools and LEAVES Write, Edit, Task, SendMessage and WebSearch despite its name; and --allowedTools Read changed NOTHING, so an allowlist does not narrow the advertised set and only an exhaustive denylist removes tools, which fails open on any tool added in a future release.  ||  RULED BY ROHAN 2026-08-28, in his own words: leave it open for now, relying on the work_dir isolation landed in nxb-031, on the stated grounds that this is acceptable WHILE NOTHING EXTERNAL DEPENDS ON NXB and it dispatches only his own work on his own machine. Recorded as OPEN and not WONTFIX deliberately: this is a ruling with a CONDITION, not a decision that the grant is safe. The condition is the exact thing that will lapse silently, because the first external consumer will not announce itself as the moment a permission ruling expired. A permissive ruling that outlives its premise is how this project's founding defect worked: a sentence that was true when written and nobody positioned to notice it stopped being true.

findings.title: Whether a failed call is observable at all is a real measured axis with no machine-readable home
findings.summary: Measured [nxb-029]: when a refusal is NOT reported as a refusal, Claude Code still emits a tool_result with is_error true and a non-zero exit, which the model does not author, while the full 6-frame Codex trace of a sandbox denial contains no event for the denied write at all. That difference decides whether a broker can tell 'the work failed' from 'the work happened', and it is what h3's turn_failed and no_output_file reasoning actually depends on. It was carried as an opaque_tool_failure token inside REFUSAL_SCOPE, which was the wrong home: a negative answer in a list of positives, removed in nxb-034. The fact now survives only in prose.
findings.closes_when: Failure observability has its own machine-readable representation, published in the contract rather than born in code, decided together with REFUSAL_SCOPE and the embargoed terms as one decision rather than three.
findings.note: DELIBERATELY NOT GIVEN A FIELD TODAY. nxb-034 was bounded to the token fix, the contract is under embargo until the blind arm reports, and a new in-code capability field would be a fifth vocabulary born in code, which is the ruling this task sits under. Recording the gap is the whole action. Prose homes meanwhile: spawned_child.refusal_signal, W3-9's summary, and docs/REFUSAL-SIGNAL-nxb-029.md.

findings.title: An interrupted dispatch poisons its key and reports DID_NOT_HAPPEN for work that did happen
findings.summary: Found by USE, not audit, on the first real dispatch. `nxb run` prints its dispatch_key before the work so an interrupted call can retry. When the call was actually interrupted mid-flight, retrying with that key returns REFUSED / already_spawned / DID_NOT_HAPPEN, permanently. TWO layers assert it: nxb/h2.py:69 returns spawn_status DID_NOT_START and nxb/roundtrip.py:103 returns dispatch_status DID_NOT_HAPPEN. BOTH ARE SELF-CONTRADICTORY ON THEIR FACE: the guard at nxb/h2.py:68 is `spawn_for(parent) is not None`, so control reaches that branch ONLY because a spawn row EXISTS. The one branch where the broker holds direct evidence a child ran is the branch that reports it did not. That matters because dispatch_status was singled out in nxb-019 as the least ambiguous field in the vocabulary. The work is UNREACHABLE, NOT LOST: spawn_for returns the row carrying runtime_ref, and evidence_for(runtime_ref) resolves it to the child's transcript on disk. VERIFIED against the real poisoned key nxb-95ac342055ad: the killed child's transcript is 19913 bytes and resolves cleanly. Nothing exposes it, because outbox.put happens only AFTER the drain, so `nxb collect` returns UNKNOWN_KEY.
findings.closes_when: No return asserts DID_NOT_START or DID_NOT_HAPPEN on a branch whose own guard proves a spawn row exists, AND the already_spawned refusal hands the operator the runtime_ref it already holds. The status value itself is a vocabulary change and belongs in the post-embargo batch with REFUSAL_SCOPE and FAILURE-VISIBILITY-HOMELESS.
findings.note: EXPOSURE FIXED, VOCABULARY DELIBERATELY NOT. The already_spawned refusal now carries runtime_ref and the resolved transcript path, so the work is reachable; verified against a reproduced poisoned key. spawn_status stays DID_NOT_START and dispatch_status stays DID_NOT_HAPPEN, and BOTH ARE KNOWN TO BE WRONG: control reaches that branch only because a spawn row exists, so it is the one place the broker holds direct evidence a child ran. The honest value is a new vocabulary term and vocabulary is embargoed until the blind arm reports, so inventing one here would pre-empt a decision that is not a worker's to make. Flagged in code at both layers.

findings.title: A waiver for a token being REMOVED could not expire
findings.summary: Every waiver in tests/adapter_conformance_waivers.json expires by becoming CONFORMANT: an unpublished term gets published, an orphan gets emitted. A token waived because it is being DELETED has no such condition, because it was never published and there is nothing for it to become conformant with. opaque_tool_failure was waived in nxb-032b with the text 'if this waiver is still here after that lands, the removal did not happen', and when nxb-034 removed the token nothing would have noticed. The waiver would have sat there being true about nothing, which is the same shape as the orphan vocabulary terms this guard was built to find.
findings.closes_when: A waiver for a token that no code-side vocabulary carries any more is reported as stale, so removal is an expiry condition rather than a silent no-op.
findings.note: Found by me against my own instrument and reported in the nxb-032b report before it was filed; Orchestrator 2 was right that a report-only mention gets lost. The fix was proven against the REAL stale waiver rather than a synthetic one: the new rule was added first, failed naming opaque_tool_failure, and only then was that waiver deleted. The rule lives in one place, test_vocabulary_drift.stale_code_side_waivers, shared by the test and by this check, because a second copy of an anti-drift rule would drift.

findings.title: codex_evidence_verifier is trivially bypassable by any pre-existing readable file
findings.summary: Unanchored substring containment plus an attacker-chosen runtime_ref defeats the only remaining verification gate with NO write access and nothing runtime-specific. `ref not in os.path.basename(path)` and `ref in handle.read(...)` are both plain substring tests, and ref is attacker-supplied, so a short common ref matches almost any regular file on the host. VERIFIED by me: {'evidence_path':'/etc/hosts','runtime_ref':'o'} returns True, as do /etc/passwd with 's', /etc/shells with 'e', and /etc/hosts with 'host'. There is no minimum length or entropy check on ref and no requirement that evidence_path lie under any runtime-controlled directory.
findings.closes_when: A proof is accepted only when evidence_path is confined to the runtime's own session root AND ref is matched with anchoring or a minimum shape, so an unrelated host file cannot satisfy it.
findings.note: Closed three ways, because one would have left the shape alive: a ref must be at least 8 characters, must appear ANCHORED as a whole token in the basename rather than as a substring, and the path must resolve inside the named runtime's own evidence root. An unknown runtime fails closed.

findings.title: The FIFO protection HANDOFF celebrates as guaranteed is reopened by a stat/open race
findings.summary: nxb/proof.py checks os.stat then S_ISREG, and LATER calls open(path) on the same path, with no fstat on the opened handle. The pair is not atomic, so an attacker controlling the directory can pass a regular file to the stat and have the path resolve to a FIFO by the time open() runs, blocking the dispatch gate forever. VERIFIED structurally: the source contains os.stat(path) and a later open(path,...) and does NOT contain fstat. This DIRECTLY FALSIFIES the HANDOFF section 'CONVERT ACCIDENTAL PROPERTIES INTO GUARANTEED ONES', which records the FIFO hang as closed and converted from accidental to guaranteed. It is guaranteed against a STATIC FIFO only, never against a swap, and the section reads as though the class were closed.
findings.closes_when: The regular-file check and the read happen on the SAME file description, e.g. open first then fstat the handle, so no path swap can sit between them. HANDOFF's claim is corrected in the same change, because a celebrated false claim is worse than the bug.
findings.note: The path is opened O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK so a FIFO cannot hang the call, and S_ISREG is now an fstat on THE DESCRIPTOR ABOUT TO BE READ. A check on a path can be raced; a check on a descriptor cannot. HANDOFF's 'CONVERT ACCIDENTAL PROPERTIES INTO GUARANTEED ONES' section CLAIMED THIS EXACT PROPERTY AS ALREADY GUARANTEED and was wrong; it is corrected in place in the same change, because a celebrated false claim is worse than the bug.

findings.title: A NUL byte in evidence_path escapes the OSError handler and crashes the gate
findings.summary: os.stat raises ValueError, not OSError, on an embedded null character, and nxb/proof.py catches only OSError. VERIFIED by me: {'evidence_path':'/tmp/evidence\x00x','runtime_ref':'x'} raises ValueError: stat: embedded null character in path, escaping the function uncaught. A one-line payload aborts whatever wraps the sole remaining verification gate. Same family as H2-3, where a _kill handler caught too narrow a class and let the raise escape.
findings.closes_when: codex_evidence_verifier returns False for every input, including a malformed path, and never raises. Its callers were promised a boolean.
findings.note: os.stat raises ValueError, not OSError, on an embedded NUL. Same family as H2-3, where the kill path caught too narrow a class. Both handlers now catch (OSError, ValueError).

findings.title: The 256KB evidence read cap may reject genuine late-appearing refs
findings.summary: A child flagged that a transcript whose ref first appears beyond the 256KB read cap would fail verification, and named its own uncertainty rather than asserting it. MEASURED in nxb-040 across 582 real artefacts, restricted to files the verifier would actually accept: codex n=363 max first-occurrence offset 143 bytes, claude_code n=219 max 255 bytes, none absent. Both runtimes put the ref in the first record, so the worst observed case uses 0.1% of the cap and the invariant holds with a 1000x margin.
findings.closes_when: Either an artefact is found whose ref appears only past the cap, or the invariant that the ref is always in the first record is stated and checked.
findings.note: Closed by the SECOND branch of its own closes_when, stating and checking the invariant, rather than by WONTFIX. The check deliberately does not re-measure the machine, because a regression test that depends on whichever transcripts happen to exist would be measuring the environment. It asserts the cap stays far above the measured worst case, since lowering it is the only way this becomes real and is a code change a test can watch. First measurement was wrong and is recorded as such: counting every .jsonl basename as a ref pulled in subagent transcripts, which are not session artefacts, and reported a 96KB offset and 240 not-found. Restricting to the files evidence_for actually returns gave the numbers above. RESOLVED nxb-037. Closed by measurement rather than by giving it an owner: it was the last unowned finding, and assigning a plausible-but-unmeasured concern to someone is how a backlog grows work that measurement would have deleted. If the ref's position ever moves, verification fails and the canary says so loudly, so no extra guard is needed.
findings.reason: MEASURED, NOT ARGUED. The cap stays at 256KB. Across 582 real artefacts on this machine, codex rollouts and claude_code transcripts, the ref appeared within the cap EVERY TIME and the worst first-offset was 255 BYTES, three orders of magnitude inside it. The concern was plausible and is not a defect on any observed data, so raising the cap would buy nothing and would widen the read an attacker-supplied path can cause. Evidence: evidence/nxb-037/proof4-read-cap.json.
findings._landing_note: Authored by Worker 3 under nxb-037. It landed in 109ff3a, a Worker 1 nxb-040 commit, because it was sitting uncommitted in the shared tree when they committed FINDINGS.json. Nothing was lost and this is the THIRD unattributed landing today in the same shared-tree coupling, the previous two in the other direction. Recorded as data because a record nobody can rewrite beats a message nobody re-reads, and because the remedy has to work when it is YOUR work being absorbed, not only when it is someone else's.

findings.title: A shared Ledger raises across threads, and dispatch documents that it never raises
findings.summary: MEASURED, evidence/nxb-030/. Four dispatchers with SEPARATE Ledger objects against one database file wrote 60 of 60 receipts with no errors (busy_timeout 5000 absorbs it at that volume; journal_mode is `delete`, not WAL). Four dispatchers sharing ONE Ledger object across threads wrote 0 of 60: every thread raised sqlite3.ProgrammingError, because nxb/ledger.py calls sqlite3.connect() without check_same_thread=False. nxb/dispatch.py:90 documents dispatch as 'Always returns one of three shapes, never raises.' The totality clause is scoped to INPUTS and this is a threading misuse, so it is not that clause violated on its own terms. It is worse in one way and better in another: better because no input can trigger it, worse because the caller who triggers it is the broker's own stated purpose. HANDOFF's first line is that this exists to let ONE orchestrator dispatch to agents across different runtimes AT ONCE.
findings.closes_when: EITHER the broker is single-threaded BY CONTRACT and says so loudly, refusing cross-thread use with its own error instead of leaking a sqlite internal, OR concurrent dispatch is actually safe. Both are acceptable; silence is not, because today the answer is discoverable only by hitting it.
findings.note: FILED LATE, AND THE LATENESS IS THE POINT. Measured by the orchestrator on 2026-08-28 and written into docs/PRODUCTION-GAP-nxb-030.md, then NOT filed here for several hours, while that same orchestrator quoted 'DETECTION WAS NEVER THE BOTTLENECK' and 'prose in a report is not a record' at three workers. A doc is prose; this ledger is the tracked record, and the gap between them is exactly the gap that finding describes. Caught only by grepping FINDINGS.json for my own measurement while doing something else. Nothing would have caught it otherwise, which is the argument for a guard rather than for trying harder. SETTLED nxb-038, option one: SINGLE-THREADED BY CONTRACT. Re-measured before deciding rather than working from the summary. Cross-thread use now raises LedgerThreadError naming the constraint, the remedy and the ledger path, in place of sqlite3.ProgrammingError which pointed at the wrong layer. Every public Ledger method is guarded, not just the first one, and a test asserts that. Option two was declined: nobody has asked for in-process concurrency, and the supported pattern, one Ledger per thread or process on one path, is MEASURED to work at 800 of 800 across 16 threads. dispatch()'s totality claim is now scoped to envelopes and names both storage conditions that raise through it. NOTE the closes_when's two options did not cover everything: see CONC-2.

findings.title: `nxb run --runtime codex` was dead: no declaration shipped
findings.summary: The Codex adapter existed, the CLI knew it, and contract/runtimes/ contained only claude_code.json, so F-1 refused the runtime and half the product was unreachable. Search: every json in contract/runtimes/ and every runtime_id in them. Found while verifying that start_new_session had not broken the real runtimes, which is the only reason it surfaced.
findings.closes_when: Every runtime with an adapter has a registrable declaration built from measurement.
findings.note: The disagreement thesis needs two runtimes and only one was reachable from the surface. Every value in the new declaration is measured from nxb-002 and nxb-010 or explicitly null with a reason; refusal_signal and progress_signal are MEASURED_ABSENT, not unmeasured.

findings.title: The multi-PROCESS pattern this broker blesses can still raise, and CONC-1's fix does not cover it
findings.summary: MEASURED nxb-038, evidence/nxb-038/. CONC-1 offered two options and both were about THREADS. Separate Ledger objects on one file, which is the pattern the project explicitly endorses and which F3 exists to make safe, is NOT covered by a single-threaded contract, because each Ledger is used from exactly one thread. It holds at measured volume: 4x15 wrote 60/60, 8x50 wrote 400/400, 16x50 wrote 800/800, all with zero errors in under a second. But it holds because busy_timeout 5000 absorbs the contention, not because the design excludes it. Squeezing busy_timeout on the identical shape produces the cliff: at 200ms, 551 of 800 rows and sqlite3.OperationalError('database is locked'); at 20ms, 302 of 800. The raise aborts the rest of that worker's loop, so receipts are lost silently rather than refused, and it raises through dispatch() exactly as CONC-1's case did.
findings.closes_when: Either the contention failure is bounded by design rather than by a timeout constant (WAL, or a single writer), or the raise is converted into an honest non-delivery the caller can act on, or the ledger's supported concurrency is stated as a measured limit rather than left as an absorbed accident.
findings.note: NOT FIXED IN nxb-038, deliberately. It is not reachable at any volume this project has produced, and the two obvious fixes are both machinery: WAL changes the on-disk format, and catching OperationalError would turn an infrastructure failure into a REFUSED envelope, which is a different lie because the envelope was fine and the work did not happen. An honest non-delivery term is contract vocabulary and is under the blind-arm embargo. So this is recorded with its numbers and left, which is what the orchestrator asked for when it said to say so rather than leave it implied.

findings.title: collect_report accepts `declaration` and reads it nowhere
findings.summary: nxb/h3.py:101 collect_report takes `declaration` as a REQUIRED keyword-only parameter and never reads it; nxb/roundtrip.py:129 dutifully passes it. WD-1's exact shape, found by the guard built for WD-1's class. Behaviourally harmless today, which is the point: the capability record it looks like it should carry is computed separately at roundtrip.py:181 via refusal_scope(declaration), so nothing is lost. WD-1 was also harmless-looking until Popen had no cwd=.

Waived rather than left red because a low-severity permanent red is how a suite gets muted, per this file's own _states note.

findings.title: Nothing records live process groups, so a stray outlives the broker that made it
findings.owner: Rohan: a decision, either mechanism or recorded acceptance
findings.summary: H2-8's isolation makes killing a subtree POSSIBLE and does nothing for a stray whose PARENT IS ALREADY GONE. A child's pgid is captured on the Popen object in memory and nowhere else, so if the broker dies between spawn and kill, the orphaned group has no handle anywhere and the pattern-kill ban forbids the one method that could still find it. A restarted broker cannot reap what its predecessor left. The ban plus isolation covers the case where the broker is alive to do the reaping, which is the common case and not all of them.
findings.closes_when: EITHER live process groups are recorded somewhere durable, so a restarted broker can reap its predecessor's leavings, OR the decision not to is recorded with its reason. Both close it. At current scale, accepting it may well be right.
findings.note:
FILED AFTER DECLINING TO, and the orchestrator was right to push back. I withheld it on the grounds that a finding nobody can close is a complaint, having in the SAME TASK re-owned W3-10 by giving it a closes_when a DECISION can satisfy. I applied the remedy to someone else's finding and not to my own observation. The inconsistency is the point: a real property of the system was living only in a message to one orchestrator, which is exactly what the attribution fix in 832e1e2 was about.

It is a correction to this project's own claim that the pattern-kill ban became costless once isolation landed. It did not, and HANDOFF carried that overstatement until a58bdb5.
