Recorded as data because a record nobody can rewrite beats a message nobody re-reads, and because the remedy has to work when it is YOUR work being absorbed, not only when it is someone else's.

findings.title: nxb cannot dispatch a blind arm: its own report contract names the project
findings.summary: nxb/h3.py:directive_for() appends '--- NEXUS BRIDGE REPORT CONTRACT ---' to EVERY dispatched prompt, plus prose naming 'the broker' and describing sandbox refusals. So any worker dispatched through this broker is told the project's name and that it is inside a broker system. That is exactly the class of information contract/contract.json was sanitised to remove in nxb-013 and nxb-016, where a redaction stripped module paths, a runtime capability sheet and a live participant's name, and where the audit specifically noted checking that the project's own NAME does not leak. DISCOVERED by trying to run the blind arm THROUGH nxb, which was the obvious move and would have contaminated the most expensive claim this project will make. The arms were run with direct spawns instead.
findings.closes_when: Either the report contract is stated without naming the project or the system (the report SHAPE is what the runtime needs; the branding is not), or the broker has a documented blind-dispatch mode that omits it, so a blinded task can be dispatched through the product rather than around it.
findings.note: The wider point is worth more than the fix. This is the FIRST measured case where using the product would have damaged the work, and it was invisible until someone tried. It also means the broker cannot currently run the experiment that tests the premise the broker exists to serve. Related: the sanitisation discipline in docs/BLIND-ARM-AUDIT-nxb-013.md scoped its sweep to the CONTRACT and never to the PROMPT WRAPPER the broker adds at dispatch time, which is a second surface nobody audited.

findings.title: F-10 and R-051 require different dedup keys
findings.summary: Found by Arm B (Codex) from reading alone; MISSED by Arm A, which looked straight at F-10, noticed its undefined term, and did not see the contradiction. F-10 requires deduplication on receipt_id; R-051 requires a repeated dispatch_key to resolve to the ORIGINAL receipt, which is a lookup by dispatch_key. Two conforming implementations can key idempotency differently and both cite the contract.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states one dedup key and reconciles F-10 with R-051 explicitly.

findings.title: F-2 is classified as a rule a schema cannot express, and a schema expresses it
findings.summary: Arm A. The contract lists F-2 among invariants a schema cannot express, but every field in capability_declaration is already required: true, so ordinary schema validation covers it entirely. A hand-enforced invariant that generic validation already enforces invites an implementer to write a second, divergent check.
findings.closes_when: F-2 is either removed from the hand-enforced list or restated as the thing a schema genuinely cannot express.

findings.title: Invariants F-3 and F-4 are absent from the numbering
findings.summary: Arm A. The invariant list skips F-3 and F-4 with no note. A reader cannot tell whether they were deleted, renumbered, or omitted by mistake, and an implementer auditing coverage against the numbering has no way to know it is complete.
findings.closes_when: The numbering is contiguous, or the gaps carry a line saying what happened to them.

findings.title: F-10 forbids deduplicating on a task_id no schema defines
findings.summary: Arm A. F-10 prohibits keying dedup on task_id. No schema in the contract defines a task_id field. The prohibition is meaningful history from the old system and reads to a fresh implementer as a reference to a field they must have missed.
findings.closes_when: F-10 either names the field it is warning about as historical, or the term is removed.

findings.title: A key refused for an environmental reason replays that refusal after the cause is fixed
findings.summary: Arm B, from the contract. A dispatch_key that first drew runtime_unregistered continues to draw it after the runtime is registered, because the refusal is bound to the key rather than to the condition. Refusals about the ENVELOPE (digest, count) are correctly permanent; refusals about the ENVIRONMENT are not, and the contract does not distinguish them. Sits beside RT-2: same shape, a key made permanently unusable by a transient condition.
findings.closes_when: The contract distinguishes refusals that are properties of the envelope from refusals that are properties of the environment, and says which are replayed.

findings.title: registration_unproven_capability is in the vocabulary and no rule triggers it
findings.summary: Arm A. The term is published in the refusal vocabulary but no invariant or rule produces it, so an implementer cannot tell when to emit it and a consumer cannot tell what it would mean. ORCHESTRATOR TRIAGED THIS AS A RE-CONFIRMATION; it is not. No finding covered it.
findings.closes_when: Either a rule produces it, or it leaves the vocabulary.

findings.title: Schemas are silent on unknown fields and the two arms read them oppositely
findings.summary: THE LIVE DISAGREEMENT, and the clearest single product of the experiment. Given an envelope with an unknown extra field, Arm A read the schemas as CLOSED and refused it; Arm B read them as OPEN and accepted it, citing the empty forbidden_fields list as support. Both cite the contract. This is not two models finding different defects, it is two models reading one document and disagreeing about what it says, and today an envelope's acceptance depends on which implementation receives it. No existing finding covered it.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states whether unknown fields are permitted, and what forbidden_fields being empty means.

findings.title: A null capability must carry a reason, and the contract's own example carries none
findings.summary:
FOUND BY BOTH ARMS INDEPENDENTLY. capability_declaration's doc states that a capability the runtime lacks is explicitly null WITH A REASON, never omitted, while the example immediately below sets four fields to bare null with no reason. Arm B went further and connected it to F-1: the example sets start_signal: null, and F-1 requires the broker to REFUSE such a declaration, so the contract's own example is unregistrable under its own rule.

THIS WAS KNOWN AND NEVER FILED. nxb-016 found it while sanitising the contract and deliberately did not fix it, correctly, because repairing a defect during sanitisation deletes a finding the blind arm exists to discover. That reasoning was right and the sealed prediction was confirmed. But it was recorded in a doc and a commit message and NEVER ENTERED HERE, so for the whole embargo it existed only as prose. Triaged as a re-confirmation by the orchestrator on the same assumption.
findings.closes_when: The example carries reasons for its nulls, or the doc stops requiring them, and F-1's interaction with the example is resolved.
findings.note: Filed by the worker who found it in nxb-016 and recorded it in the place that does not count. Same shape as CONC-1's lateness: prose in a report is not a record, and the person quoting that rule is not exempt from it.

findings.title: Unicode normalisation is still unspecified, and a test vector now camouflages it
findings.summary:
NEITHER ARM REACHED THIS, which is the point. Both wrote detailed canonicalisation findings against the pinned contract and neither raised normalisation; verified against both raw streams with word-boundary matching for nfc, nfd, normalis, normaliz, combining, precomposed and U+0301: ZERO hits in either. Arm B put an accented character in its own worked example and discussed only key order.

WORSE IN THE CURRENT CONTRACT THAN IN THE PINNED ONE. nxb-024 published canonicalisation.steps, which fully specify key order, whitespace, escaping and encoding, and say NOTHING about normalisation. Its test vector uses a DECOMPOSED e+U+0301 and is self-consistent with the steps, which I verified rather than assumed. But a precomposed U+00E9, which is what a keyboard produces, canonicalises to [{"s":"\u00e9"}] against the vector's [{"s":"e\u0301"}]: two payloads a human reads as identical produce two digests, and both implementations conform. The vector contains an accented character, so a reader sees the encoding question apparently addressed and stops looking.
findings.closes_when: canonicalisation.steps specify a normalisation form, or state that none is applied and that callers must agree out of band.
findings.note: Reproduction: canonicalise [{'s': NFC('e-acute')}] and [{'s': NFD('e-acute')}] by the published steps; digests 73bc74d606980f90 and a937e576ff2e8590. This is the documented shared blind spot surviving a cross-model blind test AND being camouflaged by the fix for C-1.

findings.title: Blind arms were run against a contract two commits stale, and one finding is superseded
findings.summary: The arms were pinned at 378d641 while HEAD had moved on by nxb-021 and nxb-024, 10924 bytes against 14027, so 28 percent of the current contract did not exist for them. One headline result is affected: the canonicalisation agreement re-confirms a gap that nxb-024 had already closed. Everything else checked still holds against current text: UNKNOWN, forbidden_fields, the F-3/F-4 gap, registration_unproven_capability and the undefined task_id all appear identically in both versions.
findings.closes_when: A blind arm is pinned at the contract it is being asked about, or the report states the lag and which findings it supersedes.
findings.note: Not a criticism of running the arms; pinning was correct and necessary. The gap is that nothing reconciled the pin against HEAD when the results were read.

findings.title: Which divergence wins when digest and count both fail is unspecified
findings.summary: Found by BOTH arms independently. An envelope whose declared_digest AND declared_count are both wrong can be refused as digest_divergence or as count_divergence, and the contract does not say which. Both arms chose digest and BOTH explicitly named count as equally defensible, which is the strongest form of this evidence: not that they guessed differently, but that each knew the other reading was available and the contract did not decide. A consumer keying on the reason gets a different answer from two conforming implementations. No existing finding covered it.
findings.closes_when: contract.json states the precedence when more than one refusal applies to the same envelope.

findings.title: C-6's removal left the field in the contract's own example, and the self-validation suite cannot see it
findings.summary: nxb-042 closed C-6 by removing last_proven_at from schemas.capability_declaration and from both runtime declarations, citing the dropped-value class (WD-1/WD-3) as the reason to do schema and data together. It remains at examples.capability_declaration.last_proven_at = null, so the contract's own example carries a field its schema no longer defines. VERIFIED: 'last_proven_at' in CONTRACT['examples']['capability_declaration'] is True while 'last_proven_at' in CONTRACT['schemas']['capability_declaration']['fields'] is False. THE INTERESTING HALF IS WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: tests/test_contract_selfvalidating.py passes 9 tests / 77 subtests, because nxb.contract.validate() treats schemas as OPEN. It accepts the stale example AND an invented field named totally_invented_field. So the suite whose stated job is proving the published contract validates under its own validator cannot detect a field the contract publishes and does not define.
findings.closes_when: The example carries only fields the schema defines, AND the self-validation suite would FAIL if it did not. The second half is the one that matters; removing the field without closing the hole leaves the next stale example equally invisible.
findings.note: This is BLIND-8 live in our own tree, which is what makes it worth more than a leftover. Both blind arms found the contract silent on unknown fields and read it OPPOSITELY: Arm A closed and refused an envelope with an extra field, Arm B open and accepted it, citing the empty forbidden_fields list. Our implementation is open, and that choice is why this residue is undetectable. Deciding BLIND-8 therefore decides whether this class is catchable at all. Note also that the example is a repeat offender: both arms independently found it setting bare nulls that its own doc forbids, and it now also carries an undefined field.

findings.title: A dispatched worker could enumerate and message the operator's whole fleet
findings.summary: Under the narrow default grant a child called ListAgents and enumerated ELEVEN live sessions by name and ref, then EXECUTED SendMessage, with zero permission_denied frames and an empty permission_denials. `--restricted` is a CATEGORY filter and these tools are not in the category. Because the operator's fleet runs in bypass mode, any session so messaged acts on the message without prompting: a confused-deputy path from an isolated worker into the whole fleet.
findings.closes_when: Fleet-reaching tools are banned under every grant AND the ban is verified against the child's own init frame, so a denylist that rots on a future release fails loudly.
findings.note:
TWO HALVES, and the second is the load-bearing one. A denylist alone FAILS OPEN on anything added in a future release, which is the rot the grants file already warned about. So the ban is paired with a read-back at spawn: the child's OWN init frame is checked and the dispatch is REFUSED with grant_violation if a banned tool survived. Same discipline as reading permissionMode back rather than trusting the flag, after --permission-mode manual was measured accepted and inert.

MEASURED, not inferred. Default grant went 27 tools to 9, zero banned survivors, ListAgents and SendMessage gone, and a real MCP round trip still returns 196 for 14x14. The read-back was proven by SIMULATING THE ROT: an adapter that sets the ban and omits the flag was refused and killed, naming the survivors. Watched failing rather than inferred.

ToolSearch is banned as an ESCALATION VECTOR: it surfaces and makes callable tools that were deferred, which is a route back to everything else on the list.

HONEST LIMIT: under the `shell` grant a worker has Bash and can invoke the runtime binaries directly. NO DENYLIST CONTAINS A WORKER WITH A SHELL. The ban applies there and removes the easy path; `shell` should be read as trusting the worker, not containing it. Stated in the operator note rather than left to be discovered.

findings.title: A plain process cannot inject into a live pane, and a claimed from_mode is ignored
findings.summary: MEASURED, four configurations, one outcome. A plain Python sender writing to a live pane's socket gets peer_message_status status=held within 0.17s, reason 'held for the recipient user's approval (permission-mode parity)', and the message NEVER REACHES THE MODEL. Held with no from_mode; held with from_mode 'bypassPermissions', so THE CLAIMED MODE IS IGNORED; held against a DEFAULT-mode recipient, so the recipient's mode is irrelevant too; and confirmed from the receiving side by Orchestrator 2 probing its own session, which saw nothing arrive. So 'parity' does not describe it: a sender that is not itself a recognised Claude session is held whatever either side claims.
findings.closes_when: Either a non-Claude process has a supported way to deliver into a pane, or the design stops requiring one and the docs say a broker cannot be a dispatcher.
findings.note: TWO-SIDED FINDING. As a DESIGN constraint it is fatal to broker-initiated dispatch and forced the worker-side-enforcement ruling now at nxb-049. As a SECURITY property it is the good news GRANT-1 was missing: a local process cannot spoof its permission mode to reach a pane's model. UNVERIFIED and it matters: whether a held message is releasable by the recipient approving it, and whether that approval persists. Not driveable from a script. If it releases and persists the constraint softens; nobody should assume either way. Evidence docs/PANE-TRANSPORT-nxb-047.md.

findings.title: The reply envelope carries the sender's name, so roster discovery needs no pid-to-name link
findings.summary: MEASURED. A real Claude session's SendMessage delivers full CONTENT to a plain socket listener, payload byte-intact, and the envelope carries from-name, from-mode, a usable return address, msg_id and hop-chain, all asserted by the transport rather than by the sender. A broker therefore learns a pane's NAME from the first message that pane sends it. Discovery is neither a directory read nor a broadcast probe; it is a side effect of any pane speaking once. This retires the pid-to-name problem two workers spent about an hour on: sockets are <pid>.sock and carry no name, and nothing links a session id to a pid.
findings.closes_when: The roster is built from received envelopes rather than from the filesystem, or the filesystem approach is documented as the inferior fallback it is.
findings.note: Recorded so a successor does not repeat the dead end: `claude -n NAME` DOES put the name in argv, verified on a spawned pane, so pid-to-name IS available read-only for panes launched named. It is simply worse than from-name in every respect. Codex has no --name equivalent; searched codex --help and codex exec --help for name, label and title.

findings.title: Whether a live pane mid-conversation honours directive_for() is untested
findings.summary: The directive shape survives the transport byte-intact, which is measured. Whether a STANDING worker, with its own context and its own conversation, actually obeys a directive generated by nxb/h3.py:directive_for() is untested, because in nxb-047 no directive ever reached a pane: every attempt was held. A fresh spawned child follows it; a pane mid-session may not, and the whole report-validation path assumes it does.
findings.closes_when: A directive reaches a live pane from an orchestrator and the reply is validated against the contract-generated schema, or the difference is documented.
findings.note: Now testable. After nxb-049 directives arrive from an orchestrator pane rather than from the broker, which is the direction proven to work in PANE-1.

findings.title: Worker-side task validation removes DRIFT, not ATTACK, and must not be described as a security boundary
findings.closes_when: The operator-facing docs and any report describing enrolment say 'drift' or 'discipline' and never 'security', 'boundary', 'authorisation' or 'prevents'.
findings.summary: Worker-side task validation removes DRIFT, not ATTACK; it must never be described as a security boundary.
findings.note: nxb-049 enrols a worker with a launch-bound system prompt telling it to refuse any directive without a valid broker-issued task id. That is enforcement by a party with nothing to gain from cheating, which is strictly better than an orchestrator policing itself. It is NOT a boundary. Three measured reasons: (1) an orchestrator pane can message a worker pane directly and the broker never sees it, because the broker is not in the dispatch path at all [nxb-047, measured three times]; (2) the rule is an instruction to a model, and a model that ignores its system prompt will act on anything, so the mechanism's own enforcement is probabilistic; (3) a worker can run the validate command and simply proceed anyway, since nothing observes the exit code but the worker. The only real refusal in this whole system is the transport's, which holds a non-session sender's message for the recipient user's approval, and that refusal is not ours and we cannot invoke it. Naming this correctly matters more than the mechanism: this project has twice shipped a guard that protected a decoy. LANDED nxb-049: contract/roster.json carries the not-a-boundary statement and docs/OPERATOR-NOTE-nxb.md states all three limits in the operator's own terms. The check now stands as a REGRESSION GUARD over that prose, which is the part that would quietly drift back toward overselling.

findings.title: mint cannot succeed today: the roster is reachable but unnameable, so the enforcement chain is inert end to end
findings.closes_when: A naming source exists and `nxb mint --worker <name>` returns an id against the real roster, with the transcript recorded.
findings.summary: mint cannot succeed today: 12 live workers are reachable, 0 nameable, so the enforcement chain is inert end to end.
findings.note: Measured just now against the real socket dir: 12 live workers reachable, 0 nameable, so `nxb mint --worker 'Worker 3'` refuses with roster_unnamed and issues no id. Every piece downstream is tested and works against an injected named roster (mint, wrong-worker refusal, forged-id refusal, revocation, CLI exit codes), but the chain has never run end to end on this machine because the first link cannot resolve a name. Sockets yield pids, not names. This is the same gap flagged in nxb-048 and it is now load-bearing rather than cosmetic: enrolment is unusable until a naming source exists. Do NOT close this by letting mint fall back to a positional guess; an id issued to the wrong pane is worse than no id. CLOSED nxb-049.2: the naming source is ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json, keyed on its own messagingSocketPath rather than the pid in the filename. Measured: 27 sockets, 12 live, 12 named; 6 declared by the user and 6 nameSource=derived, which are excluded because a name the system chose for itself is not a declaration. Chain now verified end to end against the live roster: minted nxbt-3e96bb0999634b9c for 'Worker 3', task_valid for Worker 3 (exit 0), task_wrong_worker for Worker 1 on the same id (exit 3), roster_unknown_worker and NO id for the off-roster 'rohan-7b'. Liveness stays a connect; the registry's status field is deliberately unread.

findings.title: A Codex worker has NEITHER the transport hold NOR the worker-side rule, and `codex queue` injects into a live pane with no approval
findings.summary: nxb-047's 'a plain process cannot inject into a live pane' is a property of the CLAUDE socket transport only. Codex has no equivalent, and cannot be enrolled either, so a Codex worker is unprotected on both axes.
findings.note: MEASURED 2026-08-28. `codex queue --thread <uuid> --message ...` run from an ordinary shell was delivered into a live Codex TUI pane and acted on: the pane answered 4127, then 8264, then 3391, with NO approval prompt, no hold, and nothing shown to the operator beyond the message appearing. It does not need the app-server daemon (the control socket does not exist on this machine) and `codex agents` does not even run here. So the wall this project measured three times and designed around is not a general fact about live panes; it is one transport's behaviour. Compounding it: Codex has no --append-system-prompt, so a Codex pane cannot carry the nxb-049 validation rule either. A Claude worker has two things between a directive and action (the transport hold, and its own enrolment rule); a Codex worker has zero. That asymmetry is currently invisible in the rig's output beyond an `enrolled: false` flag, and it should be stated wherever Codex workers are offered. STATED nxb-050: contract/rig.json carries _protection_asymmetry and the operator note says in plain words that a Codex worker has neither protection, with the codex queue measurement behind it. CLOSED DIFFERENTLY IN nxb-051: not by gating codex's IPC, which is not ours to gate, but by removing reachability from the authorisation question. Dispatch is now typed for BOTH runtimes and carries a marker and a task id; anything arriving through codex queue or a pane message is UNMARKED, which the rule defines as the operator. Both runtimes now run the SAME rule, verbatim -- a test asserts the typed rule contains the launch rule -- and six live cases passed, three per runtime.
findings.closes_when: The operator note and contract/rig.json both state, in the operator's terms, that a Codex worker has neither protection, and the rig's own output marks Codex panes as unprotected rather than merely unenrolled.

findings.title: A broker that can send-keys can act as the operator, so the worker-side rule becomes the only thing left
findings.summary: tmux send-keys types into a pane as though the human did. Nothing downstream can distinguish it from Rohan typing, which is exactly why it works and exactly what makes it load-bearing.
findings.note: Filed at Orchestrator 2's request and in ENFORCE-1's terms. On Rohan's own machine, in his own tmux session, a broker typing on his behalf is legitimate -- it is him by proxy. But it removes the last thing that was NOT a model instruction: with the socket transport, an unapproved sender was held by the transport itself; with send-keys there is no hold, no sender identity, and no record that the keystroke was not his. The nxb-049 rule then stands alone, and ENFORCE-1 already says what that rule is worth: it removes drift, not attack. THE RIG DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DISPATCH. send-keys is used only to launch a pane and to type /rename, both before any work exists, and no dispatch module imports nxb.rig -- a test walks their ASTs. Making send-keys a dispatch path is a decision for Rohan, not a default to slide into, and it should be taken knowing it is the same channel whether the typist is him or a broker. nxb-051: the ruling is RECORDED in contract/rig.json as RELAYED, with heard_directly_from_rohan_by_this_worker false. This worker has never had a message from Rohan on this; it arrived through an orchestrator paraphrasing a conversation. Enough to build on, not enough to close with, so the check now requires ruling_confirmed_by_rohan.
findings.closes_when: Rohan has ruled on whether send-keys may carry dispatch, and the ruling is recorded in the contract with whatever guard it implies.

findings.title: A typed rule is a weaker KIND of barrier than a system prompt, and its decay over a long session is UNMEASURED
findings.summary: Codex carries the rule as a first conversational message. It held over three exchanges. Whether it survives fifty is not known, and nobody should assume parity with Claude's launch-bound rule.
findings.note: Both runtimes now run the same rule text, but they hold it differently. Claude's arrives via --append-system-prompt: structurally above later messages, cannot be un-read, cannot be argued out. Codex's is typed as its first message: it can be argued with, outweighed by later context, or pushed out of the window entirely. MEASURED so far: the Codex rule held across three directives (valid id, wrong-worker id, unmarked), refusing correctly on the second and treating the third as the operator. That is a real barrier working. It is ALSO a three-turn conversation, and the failure mode in question is decay over many turns, which this does not touch. DO NOT report parity between the runtimes on the strength of these six cases. The open question Rohan should have answered: which runtime forgets first, and after how many turns. A long-conversation soak is the experiment; it has not been run.
findings.closes_when: A soak has run a typed-enrolled Codex worker past a realistic conversation length and re-tested the wrong-worker case, with the turn count at which the rule decays recorded (or evidence it does not).

findings.title: A hardcoded default session name drifted from the rig actually standing, and the refusal blamed the roster
findings.summary: mint and rig send defaulted to a session literally named 'nxb' while the standing rig was 'nxb-s2'. mint refused a declared Codex worker as roster_unknown_worker without saying any rig was consulted, and rig send's remedy suggested standing up a SECOND rig. Both refusals were true in their letter and wrong in their diagnosis.
findings.note: MEASURED 2026-08-30, two commands: mint --worker 'CX Worker 1' --session nxb-s2 ISSUED on the first try (the combined roster had landed in nxb-051), while the same mint with the default refused and listed only the Claude-registry names. The cost was real: the miss was relayed into a handoff as 'mint cannot see Codex panes -- the roster reads Claude's session registry only', named THE live blocker on Rohan's pilot, and stood for a day. The class is this project's own 'two things that must agree, and nothing making them': the flag default and the session the operator stood up. Fixed by REMOVING the assumption rather than improving the default: mint counts every rig recorded next to the ledger (state files already know the population; tmux still answers per-pane liveness); rig send resolves the ONE standing rig, refuses keystroke_ambiguous_rig when two stand, and when told a session with no state its refusal names the rigs that ARE standing with the exact --session flag as remedy. Second lesson, filed in HANDOFF.md: the handoff's diagnosis was a stale claim about mutable state, and measuring it cost two commands.
findings.closes_when: No dispatch-path command assumes a session name: mint counts every recorded rig, and rig send discovers the standing rig or names the standing ones in its refusal.

findings.title: The pane path had no reply channel, so a dispatched answer was never correlated to its task and review was a habit rather than a step
findings.summary: rig send typed a directive and returned. Nothing read the answer back. An orchestrator could dispatch, never look, and report success; or read the wrong answer off a stale screen and never know, because nothing tied a reply on a pane to the task that asked for it.
findings.note: RAISED BY ROHAN, mid-demonstration, against a rep that had just succeeded: 'what if what it did was wrong? you would have never caught it as the orchestrator and that's on you.' The orchestrator HAD read the pane and independently verified the answer, but both were discipline, not mechanism, and nothing recorded either. This is the pane half of the already-recorded hole 'THE LOOP IS CLOSED FOR THE EASY RUNTIME ONLY': a spawned child returns its answer as a value, a live pane had no content reply channel. FIXED by reusing the mechanism the rig already proved for enrolment acks and rename confirmations: every automated directive now closes with a reply protocol asking for [NXB-DONE <task_id>] as the last line, and `rig collect` reads the pane back. The marker carries the TASK ID, which is the correlation nothing had. Three states, and WAITING is the honest default: a worker still thinking and a worker that REFUSED and correctly did nothing else are indistinguishable from outside, so collect returns the pane tail rather than guessing, and distinguishes dispatch_seen true (landed, in flight) from false (never landed or scrolled away). WAITING exits 4, never 0, so a script cannot mistake an absent answer for an answer, and re-collecting is free -- which is what keeps any deadline from being load-bearing. The protocol travels with the DIRECTIVE, not the enrolment rule, so it works on panes already standing and degrades correctly on a Codex pane whose typed rule has decayed (RIG-3). VERIFIED LIVE on both runtimes: CX Worker 1 (codex) and CC Worker 2 (claude_code) each answered and each answer carried its own validate call as evidence the id check ran.
findings.closes_when: A dispatched directive's answer can be read back correlated to its task id, on both runtimes, with an absent answer distinguishable from a delivered one.

findings.title: `rig clear` discarded a Codex pane's typed enrolment rule while the state kept claiming it was enrolled
findings.summary: Claude holds its rule in --append-system-prompt, which survives /clear. Codex holds it as a first conversational message, which /clear exists to discard. Nothing re-typed it and nothing downgraded the record, so a cleared Codex pane was named, addressable, recorded as enrolled, and enforcing nothing.
findings.note: The record said `enrolment: "typed"`, which describes how a rule was DELIVERED and not whether it still HOLDS. That is one field carrying two facts, which this project has already filed once as the shape that turns into a permanent wrong answer. FIXED BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by measurement, deliberately: clear() now re-types the rule after clearing and waits for the acknowledgement, so the question of whether /clear discards it stops mattering. A pane that will not re-acknowledge is DOWNGRADED to unenrolled in the state file and named in an `unprotected` list, so rig send refuses it rather than typing at a pane that no longer enforces. Also fixes the silent demotion this exposed: `role` was never persisted, so a cleared ORCHESTRATOR would have been re-enrolled with the worker rule.
findings.closes_when: clear() restores enrolment for typed panes and records any pane that cannot be re-enrolled as unenrolled, so no pane is ever recorded enrolled while not enforcing.

findings.title: The orchestrator seat was told only how to RECEIVE work, so nothing anywhere knew how to orchestrate
findings.summary: Every pane, orchestrator included, got the worker rule: 'You are the worker named Orchestrator.' Nothing told an orchestrator that mint, rig send, rig collect or the roster exist. The dispatch plumbing was complete, proven, and unreachable by any agent.
findings.note: FOUND BY ROHAN while being taught the workflow by hand, and his response is the finding: 'I am NOT going to do this by hand thats stupid and inefficient.' He is right, and it is this project's founding defect in its purest form: a capability that exists and that nothing is positioned to use. The three MCP tools registered in both runtimes (nxb_dispatch/collect/pending) all drive the headless spawn path and never touch a pane, so even a tool-using orchestrator had no route to the fleet. FIXED: enroll.py gains an orchestrator brief carrying the fleet-listing command, the three dispatch steps, the roster ceiling (stop and ask, never substitute, never silently do the work yourself), the rule that WAITING is not an answer, and the instruction to cross-check on DIFFERENT runtimes because same-runtime agreement is weak evidence. The rig types it into any pane whose role is orchestrator, and `rig orchestrate --worker X` brief a pane that is already standing so an existing fleet does not have to be rebuilt. VERIFIED LIVE: Rohan's standing Orchestrator pane was briefed and acknowledged.
findings.closes_when: An orchestrator pane is told, at stand-up and without the operator typing anything, how to list its fleet, mint, send, collect, and what to do when a worker it needs does not exist.

findings.title: tmux matches a session target by PREFIX, so `rig down` killed a rig it did not name
findings.summary: `rig down` defaulted to the name `nxb`, tmux prefix-matched the operator's `nxb-s2`, killed it, and reported "session": "nxb" -- a session that never existed.
findings.note: MEASURED 2026-09-03 with a probe session: `has-session -t zztest` returned 0 against a session named `zztest-abc`. Right outcome by luck, wrong reason, and a report naming a session that was never there. With two rigs standing whose names share a prefix it is a coin flip over which one dies, and the operator is told the wrong name either way. Every session-targeted tmux call now uses tmux's own exact-match form `=name`, verified to reject a prefix. Same class as RIG-4 and found the same way: by reading an output that did not match reality rather than by a test.
findings.closes_when: Every session-targeted tmux call uses exact matching, so a target can never resolve to a session the operator did not name.

findings.title: An unrecognised blocking prompt is indistinguishable from a slow boot, and burns the full deadline saying nothing useful
findings.summary: A Codex release landed mid-session and two of three Codex panes booted onto an update chooser. Not being in BLOCKING_PROMPTS, it read as 'not ready yet', so the rig waited out its whole 60s deadline per pane and reported rig_pane_not_ready instead of naming the obstacle.
findings.note: MEASURED on a real stand-up in front of the operator. The table now carries the update chooser's strings. The durable point is that this table is DISCOVERED, never predicted: every entry in it was added because a pane sat on a screen no amount of waiting could clear, and the next runtime release can add another. A readiness check that cannot say WHY it is not ready degrades to a sleep with extra steps.
findings.closes_when: The update prompt is recognised and refused by name with a remedy, and the contract records that blocking prompts are discovered rather than predicted.

findings.title: The trust-prompt remedy told the operator to re-run, which refuses, and it is runtime-dependent anyway
findings.summary: The remedy said 'answer the trust prompt, then re-run'. Re-running refuses because the session now exists. And a Claude pane needs no re-run at all, while a Codex pane does.
findings.note: A Claude pane is named and enrolled IN ITS LAUNCH COMMAND (-n plus --append-system-prompt), so answering the dialog lets it finish booting fully enrolled -- verified live: both CC panes came up named and enforcing after Rohan answered. A Codex pane is named and enrolled AFTER readiness by typing, and the rig has already given up by then, so it genuinely needs a rebuild. One remedy for two runtimes was wrong for both. A remedy that does not work is worse than no remedy: it spends the operator's trust as well as their time.
findings.closes_when: The remedy is runtime-specific and each branch is an instruction that actually works.

findings.title: A task id could never be invalidated: revoke existed in the class and on no command line
findings.summary: TaskRegistry.revoke() has always existed and nothing exposed it. Ids never expire and are not consumed on use, so 'I am done' left every id ever minted permanently valid: 20 of them, including ids for workers that no longer existed and rigs that had been torn down.
findings.note: Found by asking what the operator does when finished, which nobody had asked before. `nxb revoke <id> | --worker <name> | --all` now exposes it and returns the ids actually revoked, so revoking nothing is visible rather than reported as success. The 20 stale ids were revoked on 2026-09-03. NOT fixed and deliberately left open as a separate question: whether an id should be CONSUMED on use or EXPIRE, which is a contract decision rather than a missing command, and inventing a lifetime nobody has measured is what this project keeps deleting.
findings.closes_when: An operator can invalidate one id, every id for a worker, or all of them, from the command line.

findings.title: A Claude Code pane scrolls its transcript INTERNALLY, so the collector's anchor vanishes and it reported the dispatch as never having landed
findings.summary: collect_reply anchors on the end of the directive to know where the worker's own output starts. Claude Code's TUI scrolls inside itself, so once it redraws, tmux's scrollback contains no trace of the directive and the anchor is gone. Codex keeps its transcript in the terminal's scrollback and does not lose it.
findings.note: MEASURED 2026-09-03 on a live refusal: capture-pane -S -3000 returned 38 lines holding the launch command and the worker's full reply, and nothing of the directive between them. The collector reported dispatch_seen false with a detail saying it 'may never have landed', which was FALSE and would have had an orchestrator re-send work a worker had already refused. Another runtime asymmetry that would have made collect useless on half the fleet, and it was found within one dispatch of shipping. FIXED with a fallback: when the anchor is absent the done marker alone is trusted, minus the copy that lives inside the sentence requesting it -- the same collision that caused the collector's first false green. The answer's END stays exact because it is this task's own marker; its START becomes a line budget, and the result says so with anchored:false rather than presenting an approximate start as a precise one.
findings.closes_when: A collect can find an answer on a pane whose directive has scrolled away, and says plainly whether the answer's start is anchored or budgeted.

findings.title: The two runtimes ran different permission postures and nobody had decided that, which starved the orchestrator of its own fleet
findings.summary: Claude panes launched --yolo from the first day. Codex panes launched --sandbox workspace-write. One fleet, two powers, no decision behind it. The sandboxed Codex orchestrator could not reach the tmux socket in /private/tmp, so the agent whose whole job is knowing the fleet was told the fleet was empty.
findings.note: FOUND BY ROHAN, by looking at his own screen: 'all these orchestrators and workers should be in --yolo mode. this is wrong.' He was right on the policy and it also happened to be the open bug: nxb-055 had just made the empty roster loud without knowing its cause, and an orchestrator hypothesis about TMPDIR had already been tested and disproved. The sandbox is the cause the loud error would have named. TWO THINGS WORTH KEEPING. First, the asymmetry was invisible because it lived in a DEFAULT ARGUMENT -- `sandbox="workspace-write"` reads as a deliberate policy choice in a signature, and nobody had chosen it; the default is now None and a sandbox is an explicit opt-in that appears in the command on screen. Second, this is the fourth runtime asymmetry this project has found by using it rather than by testing it (enrolment binding, transcript scrolling, trust prompts, and now permission posture), and every one presented as a bug in something else. The parity is now a guard rather than a fact, because a review catches drift once and a test catches it every time.
findings.closes_when: Both runtimes launch with the fleet's declared posture by default, a lesser sandbox is an explicit opt-in visible in the launched command, and a test asserts the parity.

findings.title: A session target and a pane target have DIFFERENT exact-match forms, and sweeping one across both broke rig up entirely
findings.summary: RIG-8 replaced every session-targeted tmux call with tmux's exact form `=name`. A pane or window target rejects that and requires `=name:`, so split-window failed with "can't find pane: =nxb" and no rig could be stood up at all.
findings.note: Found by the operator on the very next `rig up`, one command after the fix that caused it. THE POINT IS NOT THE SYNTAX, IT IS WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: every other test in tests/test_rig.py mocks _tmux, so the mock agrees with whatever the author believes tmux's syntax to be. That is a measurement of the author, not of tmux -- the same shape as this project's own rule that the author's tests do not test the author. A sweep is exactly the kind of change a mocked suite cannot review, because the sweep and the mock share one assumption. TmuxTargetFormsAreREAL now drives the real binary, launches no runtime, costs milliseconds and no tokens, and covers three properties: the two exact forms, that the bare form is REJECTED for a pane target, and RIG-8's own prefix-defeating property. Proven by re-introducing the defect and watching two of its four tests fail. Second-order lesson, recorded because it cost real work: `git checkout <file>` was run on that file while the fix was uncommitted and silently discarded it.
findings.closes_when: Session and window targets use their own exact-match form, and a test exercises the real tmux binary rather than a mock that shares the code's assumptions.

findings.title: Making an unaskable tmux loud swept in a legitimate answer, so one stale state file refused every mint in the fleet
findings.summary: nxb-055 correctly separated 'tmux answered nothing' from 'tmux could not be asked'. It missed a third case: a rig TORN DOWN hours ago genuinely has no panes. mint walks every rig recorded next to the ledger, hit the morning's dead nxb-s2, and refused rig_tmux_unavailable for a fleet that was standing and healthy.
findings.note: Found by the briefed orchestrator on its first real dispatch, and the loud error diagnosed itself by naming the dead session. THE SHAPE IS WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX: this project's most reliable defect generator is recorded as 'refuse on VERIFIED FALSE, never on CANNOT VERIFY', and nxb-055 was written to honour it. It still produced a 100% refusal, because the new refusal fired on a state that is neither false nor unverifiable -- it is simply a different true answer. A binary split of a three-state world puts one real state on the wrong side, and the wrong side was the refusing one. FIXED by asking has-session FIRST, so the distinction is drawn by tmux rather than by parsing an error string, and by having mint iterate LIVE rigs rather than every rig ever recorded. Both halves are guarded: a nonexistent session must return an empty set without raising, and a session that exists but cannot be queried must still raise.
findings.closes_when: A torn-down rig contributes no workers without raising, a standing but unqueryable session still refuses, and mint considers only rigs that are actually standing.

findings.title: The enrolment rule named its environment fix in a PARENTHESIS, so a worker handed the choice fumbled it and refused valid work
findings.summary: The rule said to verify by running `python3 -m nxb validate ... (from <repo>, or with PYTHONPATH=<repo>)`. A Codex worker running from ~ hit 'No module named nxb', tried to resolve the parenthetical itself, and refused a valid directive claiming the verifier's working directory did not exist. It does exist. The rule required assembly, and the assembly failed.
findings.note: MEASURED on the first full cross-runtime dispatch: CC Worker 1 answered 13,279 files and CX Worker 1 refused. Reproduced exactly: `python3 -m nxb validate` from /Users/rohan with no PYTHONPATH gives 'No module named nxb'. THE CLASS IS THE POINT, and it is the same one that produced the trailing-period bug an hour earlier: A RULE THAT REQUIRES THE READER TO ASSEMBLE A WORKING COMMAND HAS AN ASSEMBLY STEP, AND AN ASSEMBLY STEP FAILS. Every command in both rules is now one literal self-contained line carrying its own PYTHONPATH, needing no cd and no setup. Note the direction of the failure, which is the design working: the worker refused rather than proceeding unvalidated. SECOND DEFECT, caught by an existing guard before it shipped and strictly worse than the first: putting those commands on their own lines made the Claude LAUNCH command multi-line, and `tmux send-keys` sends a newline as a KEYSTROKE -- probed, `echo AAA\necho BBB` ran the first and stranded the second -- so `rig up` would have typed a truncated `claude --yolo -n 'X' --append-system-prompt 'You are the worker...` fragment and run the rest as shell. No rig could have stood up. The shell command is now flattened while the TYPED rules keep their newlines, because a composer treats a newline as a line break and a shell treats it as go. One string, two destinations, one of which means 'execute now'.
findings.closes_when: Every command in both rules is a single self-contained line carrying its own environment, and the launch command is asserted to contain no newline.

findings.title: RIG-7 was fixed only on the typed half, so a Claude orchestrator would have launched carrying the WORKER rule
findings.summary: launch_command ignored `role` entirely for claude_code and always called enroll_command, which always built the worker rule. The orchestrator brief reached a pane only through the TYPED path, which only Codex uses.
findings.note: Found by READING the function when Rohan asked for a Claude orchestrator, before it could waste a stand-up. The defect survived because every rig ever stood up happened to seat Codex in the orchestrator chair, so the claude_code branch of a role decision had never once been taken. Same shape as DECL-1, already recorded here: THE MOST-USED PATH HIDES THE LEAST-USED ONE, and the thing that was 'already working' is the thing that was dead. Two guards now cover both directions: a Claude orchestrator must get the orchestrator brief, a Claude worker must not.
findings.closes_when: launch_command honours role on every runtime, and tests assert both directions on the claude_code path.

findings.title: The fleet's shape was a hardcoded table with one entry, so composition was a code change
findings.summary: SCENARIOS held exactly one scenario, in Python. An operator wanting one Claude orchestrator over five Codex workers, or two workers, or six, had to edit the source.
findings.note: Rohan: 'the point is we need it configurable'. THE TABLE WAS THE ONLY LIMIT -- everything below it already handled any mix of runtimes and roles, so this was a surface, not a rebuild. `--orchestrator cc --workers cx:5` composes a scenario at the prompt; `parse_workers` accepts short forms because a composition is typed by hand. Composition belongs to the operator for the same reason the roster does: the population is declared by the person who will watch it.
findings.closes_when: An operator can compose an arbitrary fleet shape from the command line without editing Python.

findings.title: Two standing rigs share worker names, and mint would have issued a ticket into the wrong fleet
findings.summary: Scenario-built fleets name workers by runtime and index, so two rigs both contain 'CX Worker 1'. mint combined every standing rig's roster and would have minted against whichever was enumerated first.
findings.note: Found by standing a second rig, which is the test Rohan asked for. A ticket names a WORKER, not a rig, so a ticket minted while thinking of one fleet types into another -- and both would validate, because the worker's own check only asks whether the id names it. Closed on both sides: mint REFUSES roster_ambiguous_worker naming each rig, and every dispatch command in the orchestrator brief now carries --session, so an orchestrator can only reach its own fleet. The brief also states the hazard in the operator's terms rather than relying on the flag being present. VERIFIED with two rigs standing: an unscoped mint refused with both rig names, a scoped one issued. SUPERSEDED BY RIG-20 the same day, at Rohan's direction: 'you just change the name from that simple ass name CX Worker 1 to adding the rig number to it'. He is right, and the distinction is the useful part: this finding built a GUARD where an INVARIANT belonged. A refusal that fires on ordinary operator behaviour is a design admitting it cannot make the bad state impossible. The refusal is KEPT, unreachable, because it now fires only on a naming REGRESSION, which is the one thing that could bring the collision back.
findings.closes_when: An ambiguous worker name refuses rather than guessing, and every command in an orchestrator's brief names its own rig.

findings.title: A launch-bound rule is typed through a pty that silently drops input past ~1024 bytes, and the worker rule had TEN bytes of headroom
findings.summary: The rule was embedded in the launch command and typed with send-keys. A pty in canonical mode drops input past roughly 1024 bytes. The worker rule's command was 1014. The orchestrator brief's was 3891 and had already crossed it: its command sat in the shell unsubmitted and the pane refused.
findings.note: MEASURED through send-keys: 1000 bytes arrived whole, 2000 never reached the shell at all. NOTHING ANYWHERE RECORDED THE LIMIT, so the next sentence added to the worker rule would have silently truncated the enrolment of every Claude worker in every rig -- and a truncated rule still looks like a rule. A NEAR-MISS FOUND ONLY BECAUSE ITS BIGGER SIBLING FAILED LOUDLY FIRST. Also worth recording as a discipline win: the pane capture appeared to show a corrupted rule ('You re the worker', 'if nd only if'), which read as live corruption; reading the RUNNING PROCESS'S ARGV showed it intact at 1035 bytes. capture-pane renders a screen, argv is the fact -- a false alarm avoided by checking the authority rather than the display. FIXED by writing the rule to a file the command reads, so the typed command is a fixed ~150 bytes however long the rule grows. A threshold would only move the cliff.
findings.closes_when: A launch command's length is independent of its rule's length, and a test asserts the command stays far below the pty limit for every role.

findings.title: A worker's name now carries its rig, so cross-rig collision is impossible rather than merely refused
findings.summary: Fleets are built from a shape, so every rig held a 'CX Worker 1' and every rig held an 'Orchestrator'. A ticket names a worker and not a rig, so a ticket minted for one fleet would type into another and be validated there. Names are now prefixed with their session at stand-up: 'nxb CX Worker 1', 'lab Orchestrator'.
findings.note: ROHAN'S CALL, and it replaced a guard I had just shipped. RIG-18 detected the ambiguity and refused; he asked why the name was ambiguous at all. THE DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING: a refusal that fires on ordinary operator behaviour is a design conceding it cannot make the bad state impossible, and this project already knows that a rule binding a PERSON decays while a rule binding a FILE holds -- an INVARIANT is the same idea one level up. Three consequences beyond the fix. (1) `--session` stops being needed to disambiguate anything, because there is nothing to disambiguate; send and collect now find the rig that holds the name. (2) The ORCHESTRATOR collided too and was easy to miss, since there is only ever one per rig. (3) Naming is applied at STAND-UP rather than baked into the scenarios, so a scenario stays a SHAPE and the naming rule lives in exactly one place. VERIFIED with two rigs standing: zero name overlap, and mint/send/collect ran end to end against 'lab CX Worker 1' with no session flag anywhere, answering MANGO.
findings.closes_when: Two rigs built from the same shape share no worker name, the orchestrator is scoped too, and scoping is applied in one place at stand-up.

findings.title: compose() validated the orchestrator's runtime and trusted the workers', because its only caller had already checked them
findings.summary: An unknown worker runtime reached WORKER_PREFIX and raised KeyError. From the CLI that could not happen: parse_workers validated first. The studio is a second caller that passes runtimes straight through, so the KeyError surfaced as a dropped HTTP connection rather than a refusal.
findings.note: Caught by a test written before the surface was used. A VALIDATION THAT LIVES IN THE CALLER IS ONE NEW CALLER AWAY FROM BEING ABSENT, and the arrival of a second caller is exactly when nobody re-reads the first one's guarantees. Fixed in compose, which is where the assumption is, and the refusal now NAMES the offending value because a refusal the operator cannot act on costs them the same trip as no message. The handler also catches anything unexpected and answers 500 with the reason: a dropped connection tells a page nothing and reads as the server dying.
findings.closes_when: compose refuses an unknown runtime or a count below 1 by naming the value, regardless of which caller supplied it, and no handler path can drop a connection.

findings.title: A composed fleet needs agents as individuals, not counts, and every inspector control had to reach a real flag
findings.summary: compose() builds a fleet from counts, which suits a command line and not a diagram. A drawn node is an individual: a name the operator chose, its own model, reasoning effort and directory. compose_agents takes the list as given and validates it.
findings.note: Built from a mockup Rohan brought back from a UI session. THE RULE I HELD IT TO: no control ships that the backend cannot honour, because a selector that looks like configuration and functions as a comment is this project's founding defect in a nicer font. So each was measured against the runtimes' own --help first -- claude takes --model and --effort, codex takes -m and reaches reasoning effort through the same -c key its config.toml uses -- and everything unsupported was left out rather than mocked up. Pane preview is refused in the UI with the reason stated, because an invented picture of a tmux layout is a diagram that lies. Startup instructions are typed UNMARKED and last: they are the operator briefing his own pane, so marking them would both misrepresent them and make the worker refuse its own setup for want of a task id nobody minted. VERIFIED by standing the mockup's own fleet through the API and reading the running processes: claude --model opus --effort xhigh, codex -m ... -c model_reasoning_effort, and the Claude pane reporting 'Opus 5 with xhigh effort' on its own screen.
findings.closes_when: A drawn node's name, provider, model, effort and directory all reach the launched process, and any control the backend cannot honour is absent or refuses with its reason.

findings.title: The model picker offered a model the runtime rejects, because I typed the list from memory
findings.summary: A closed dropdown listed gpt-5.6 among Codex's models. The flag plumbing was correct and the VALUE was invented: the live pane came back with a 400, 'The gpt-5.6 model is not supported'.
findings.note: Caught by reading the pane after the stand-up rather than by trusting that a green READY meant a working fleet -- the rig was READY, the pane was erroring. The distinction worth keeping: the control WORKED and its OPTIONS were wrong, which a test of the plumbing would never have caught, and a closed picker presents an invented list with the authority of a discovered one. Codex's suggestions now come from the operator's own ~/.codex/config.toml, the file that runtime already obeys; Claude's aliases are quoted from its --help. Both fields are FREE TEXT with those as datalist suggestions, so a suggestion I get wrong costs a retype instead of blocking a value that would have worked.
findings.closes_when: Model and effort are free-text fields whose suggestions are read from each runtime's own configuration rather than written from memory.

findings.title: `el.hidden = true` did nothing, because an id selector with a display outranks the browser's own hidden rule
findings.summary: The canvas placeholder set display:grid on an id. The user agent's [hidden]{display:none} loses to that on specificity, so hiding it was a silent no-op and the instruction text sat underneath every node the operator placed.
findings.note: FOUND BY ROHAN LOOKING AT IT: 'the text in the center giving instructions should disappear the second a component touches that grid. its overlapping shit.' The code was right -- `$('#empty').hidden = t.nodes.length > 0` runs on every paint -- and the CSS silently overruled it, which is why reading the JS found nothing. Fixed with a page-wide `[hidden]{display:none !important}` rather than a rule for this one element, because the trap belongs to any element that gets both an id and a display, and the next one would have inherited it. THE SAME SESSION ALSO SHOWED THE ERROR SURFACE EARNING ITS KEEP: his log strip read 'models: no such route', which is not a bug in the page at all but a server still running from before /api/models existed. A silent page would have shown empty model suggestions and left him guessing.
findings.closes_when: Hiding an element hides it regardless of what specificity its own rules carry, and a test asserts the page-wide rule is present.

findings.title: The live chip matched a node's CURRENT label, so renaming a drawn node made a working pane read as a draft
findings.summary: Liveness was `liveNames.has(rig + ' ' + node.name)`. Rename the node and the match breaks while the pane carries on working, so the diagram reported draft for something that was running.
findings.note: Nodes now carry `deployed`, stamped with the pane name at stand-up, and liveness keys on that. A node whose label has since moved on shows 'edited' rather than claiming either state, with the running name in its tooltip -- because neither 'live' nor 'draft' is true of a pane that is running under a name the drawing no longer uses. The general shape: a UI that identifies a running thing by its current DISPLAY NAME is identifying it by something the operator is free to change.
findings.closes_when: A renamed node still reports its pane as running, and says its drawing has drifted from what is deployed.

findings.title: A tab was a drawing with no way back from the machine
findings.summary: Tabs are browser drafts and rigs are tmux sessions, and nothing connected them in the direction that mattered: a rig stood up from the CLI could not be edited in the studio at all, and tearing one down from the panel left its tab claiming panes that no longer existed.
findings.note: Every standing or recorded rig now has an `open` button that reconstructs it as a tab -- names, runtimes, roles, models and efforts all come from the rig's own state rather than from anything the page remembered. Tearing a rig down clears the `deployed` stamps on the tab that drew it, so the drawing stops claiming panes that are gone. Rebuilding a standing rig now asks first and says what is lost, which was the same one-click hazard the tear-down button had.
findings.closes_when: A rig that exists can be opened into a tab, and a rig that is gone leaves no tab claiming it is running.

findings.title: Backspace deleted a node and nothing could bring it back
findings.summary: No undo. A mis-hit key destroyed a configured agent -- its name, model, effort, directory and startup instructions -- with no way back.
findings.note: Cmd/Ctrl+Z undoes, Shift+Cmd+Z redoes, over snapshots of the whole draft taken BEFORE each discrete act. The detail that makes it usable: text fields snapshot on FOCUS rather than on input, because an undo that walks back one character at a time is a typing history and not an undo.
findings.closes_when: Every mutating action is undoable, and one undo covers one edit rather than one keystroke.

findings.reason: RULED BY ROHAN, and it is a scope decision rather than a deferral. I had filed the absence of dispatch and collect from the studio as its biggest gap. His ruling: 'thats not a problem the pane should be open at all time so i can be the human gate this setup is just to architect the workflows BEFORE using them once they are created i go to tmux and work from there.' So the studio is an ARCHITECTURE surface and tmux is the working surface, deliberately. That also keeps the human gate where he wants it: work is given to a fleet in front of him, in the panes, not through a browser button that could dispatch while he is looking elsewhere.
findings.title: The studio cannot dispatch work or collect answers
findings.summary: The studio composes fleets and stands them up. Giving those agents work, and reading what they answered, happens in tmux.
findings.closes_when: Not applicable: the owner has ruled this out of scope for the studio.

findings.title: A rig record could never be removed, so the panel listed every rig ever built
findings.summary: `rig down` deliberately keeps the state file, which is how a torn-down rig stays visible and re-openable. Nothing ever deleted one. With two rigs standing the panel listed five, and after tearing both down it listed five dead ones.
findings.note: Seen the moment the operator asked for a clean slate and the panel disagreed with `tmux ls`. A record with no delete is a list that only grows, and this project already deletes rather than adds by default. `rig forget` removes one, from the CLI and from the panel's × on a DOWN rig, and REFUSES while the session is standing -- forgetting a live rig would leave a running fleet with no record naming its panes, which is the one state nothing else in this system can recover from. The refusal is server-side rather than a hidden button, so it holds regardless of what the page believes.
findings.closes_when: A dead rig's record can be removed, forgetting a standing rig is refused server-side, and forgetting nothing reports 404 rather than success.

findings.title: The model and effort fields were unusable: typing in one destroyed it, because every keystroke rebuilt the panel
findings.summary: Their oninput handler called paint(), and paint() rebuilds the inspector with innerHTML. So the input being typed into was destroyed on the first character: focus died and the suggestion list closed. The fields existed, were wired to real flags, and could not be filled in.
findings.note: ROHAN: 'currently in studio it is only default model. we need to add model selection, effort selection as well. this is imperative.' The feature was already there and already reached the runtime -- verified that same afternoon by reading `claude --model opus --effort xhigh` out of a live process -- so the natural reading of his report was that it needed building. It did not; it needed to stop eating his keystrokes. WORTH KEEPING: a feature that cannot be OPERATED is indistinguishable from a feature that does not EXIST, and my own verification could not see the difference because I tested the backend through the API and never typed into the field. The whole studio was verified that way. Fixed by splitting paint() into paintCanvas() and inspector(): text fields repaint the canvas only; selects still do a full paint, because changing the provider must re-render the panel to swap which model suggestions are offered. Also: the placeholder now names the model each runtime is actually configured with, read from settings.json and config.toml, because 'runtime default' is a word rather than an answer and an operator cannot decide whether to override a default he cannot see.
findings.closes_when: A model or effort can be typed into and kept, and the placeholder names the configured default rather than the word default.

findings.title: An invocation role was typed as a first message, which is the weaker binding this project already documents
findings.summary: Startup instructions were typed into every pane after it came up. For Claude that is strictly worse than available: it has --append-system-prompt, and a role in a system prompt cannot be argued out by a later message.
findings.note: Rohan's example is the reason it matters: 'i want CX Worker 1 in rig 2 to perform as adversarial auditor for CC Worker 1 rig 2'. An adversarial auditor is the exact role a later message would most want to talk out of its job, and RIG-3 already records that a typed rule decays over a long session. Claude now carries the role in its launch brief; Codex still gets it typed because it has no launch binding, and the pane records which it got as `role_binding: launch|typed` rather than a boolean, for the same reason enrolment does. VERIFIED LIVE on a two-agent rig: the Claude worker's brief file ends with the role text, and the Codex worker's pane shows it typed as a standing rule.
findings.closes_when: A role is bound at launch on any runtime that supports it, and each pane records which binding it received.

findings.title: The studio could not show usage, which is the thing the operator designs against
findings.summary: Rohan picks which vendor carries a fleet based on which has headroom: 'if i have lower usage on claude but high usage on codex ill design it with that in mind.' The composer showed none of it.
findings.note: MEASURED BEFORE BUILDING, because a fabricated usage figure is worse than none here -- he would design against it. Findings: CODEX PLAN USAGE IS REAL and local, in every rollout's rate_limits (used_percent, window_minutes, resets_at, plan_type). CLAUDE PLAN USAGE IS NOT AVAILABLE locally; the only rate_limit string in its transcripts is a 429 ERROR record, and its CLI exposes no usage command. That absence is reported WITH ITS REASON and a pointer to /usage, never as an empty gauge, which would read as zero. TOKENS are real for both. TWO THINGS KEPT DELIBERATELY APART: a percentage of a plan window and a count of tokens are different kinds of number, and cache reads are shown apart from input because 97.7% of the all-time Claude total is cache reads -- one combined figure would be alarming and nearly meaningless. Tokens are never converted to money, per the standing rule that consumption here may be plan quota rather than per-token billing. Measured: 3.2GB over ~1200 files, ~5.5s cold and 0.02s warm behind an mtime cache. SUPERSEDED IN PART BY STUDIO-17, the same evening: the claim that Claude plan usage is unavailable was true of DISK and false of the CLI. Its /usage answers headlessly with more than Codex records. My search was 'what is written to disk' and my claim was 'not available', which is this project's own rule about stating the search alongside a negative claim, broken by me.
findings.closes_when: The studio shows real plan usage where a runtime records it, real token counts for both, and states plainly where a number is unavailable rather than rendering an empty one.

findings.title: A role written once was lost, when it should have started a library
findings.summary: Every invocation prompt had to be retyped. Rohan: a role used once should be offered back, 'and the more we create the more we have to use in the future for future workflows.'
findings.note: Personas are MARKDOWN FILES in ~/.nxb/personas, one per role, titled with an H1. They are prose the operator writes for a model to read, so they belong somewhere he can open, edit, diff and carry to another machine -- a persona locked in a JSON blob or a browser's storage is one he cannot grep, and this project already holds that what binds a FILE is what survives. The library grows BY USE: after a rig goes up, any role not already saved is offered once, and the picker in the inspector applies a saved one. The offer is suppressed when the text already matches something saved, because a prompt that fires on a no-op is noise and noise is how a prompt gets dismissed without being read.
findings.closes_when: A role can be saved from where it is written, reapplied to any later agent, lives as an editable markdown file, and is not re-offered once saved.

findings.title: The usage scan blocked the request, so a first poll would hang for five and a half seconds
findings.summary: A cold token scan reads 3.2GB and took 5.5s inside the HTTP handler that the page polls.
findings.note: CAUGHT BY A TEST THAT TIMED OUT, not by anyone reasoning about it, which is the only reason the blocking version did not ship. A first call now starts the scan on a worker thread and answers `computing: true` immediately; the plan percentage is available on that first call regardless, since it comes from tailing one file. A page cannot distinguish a five-second handler from a dead server, and this project has a standing rule that a guard whose check sits behind a blocking call is decorative -- the same shape, one layer up.
findings.closes_when: No usage request blocks on a scan, and a cold read says it is computing rather than waiting.

findings.title: The canvas could not be panned, so a node past the edge was unreachable
findings.summary: There was no pan at all. Zoom was anchored at the origin, so zooming out did not reliably recover an off-screen node, and Fit scaled without panning, which left off-screen nodes off screen -- the exact complaint it existed to answer.
findings.note: Rohan, opening it on a second monitor: 'i cant even drag around the grid or change the sizing of any of the panes its very frustrating to work with.' Added drag-to-pan on empty canvas, two-finger scroll to pan, cmd-scroll and pinch to zoom AT THE CURSOR rather than the origin, space-drag to pan over a full canvas, and a Fit that pans as well as scales. A click that never moved still deselects, so the gestures do not fight. View state is per tab and persisted. Invisible to me because I only ever drove this through the API.
findings.closes_when: No node can be placed where the operator cannot reach it, and zoom keeps whatever is under the cursor.

findings.title: Three hardcoded column widths, and a header that clipped its own controls
findings.summary: The body was a fixed grid, so a narrower display crushed the canvas between a 224px rail and a 356px inspector with no way to give it room. The header did not wrap, so Auto layout ran off the right edge.
findings.note: A control the operator can see half of and cannot press is worse than one that is absent. Columns are now a flex row with draggable splitters, persisted per browser, double-click to reset because a splitter dragged into a corner is easy to do and hard to undo. Header, toolbar and status bar all wrap. THE SHAPE: built and verified at one window size by someone who never resized it, which is the same blind spot as STUDIO-10 where a field was verified through the API and never typed into. Twice in one day.
findings.closes_when: Panels can be resized and reset, and no control is clipped at a narrower window.

findings.title: I reported Claude usage as unavailable, having only searched the disk
findings.summary: STUDIO-12 recorded that Claude does not record plan usage on this machine. True of what it WRITES, false of what it will ANSWER: its /usage returns session, weekly and per-model percentages headlessly in about two seconds.
findings.note: Rohan proposed a standing session on another machine to poll it, a 'usage tunnel'. Not needed, and the check that showed it cost one command. THE FAILURE IS MINE AND THIS PROJECT ALREADY NAMES IT: a negative claim must state the search that produced it. My search was 'what is written to disk'; my claim was 'not available'. Those are different statements and I published the second, while writing a docstring about not fabricating usage numbers. Now fetched ON DEMAND and never polled -- each call is a full runtime turn, measured here at roughly 13k input tokens before the prompt, so polling quota would spend quota. Cached WITH ITS AGE, because a percentage with no timestamp cannot be weighed. It parses a vendor's human-readable text, so an unparsed answer returns an error rather than 0%. First reading: session 14 percent, week 74 percent, Fable 100 percent -- exactly the kind of fact that should change how a fleet is composed, and he could not see it until now.
findings.closes_when: Claude plan usage is shown when asked for, carries its age, is never polled, and fails loudly if the wording it parses changes.

findings.title: A silently-failed CSS edit shipped a broken layout: five flex children left inside a three-column grid
findings.summary: The splitters were added to the markup, making #body five children, and the CSS that should have turned it into a flex row never applied. Under the old three-column grid those five wrapped onto a second row, dropping the inspector underneath the canvas.
findings.note: ROHAN: 'just opened the new layout .. its worse. what happened?' THE MECHANISM IS THE FINDING AND IT IS NOT ABOUT CSS. The edit was a str.replace whose anchor no longer matched the file, and str.replace DOES NOT RAISE -- it returns the string unchanged and reports nothing. Other edits in the same batch asserted their anchors; this one did not, so the markup change landed and its matching style change did not. Then I verified the result by running the JS through a parser, which cannot see CSS, and shipped a page I had never looked at. Two rules this project already holds, both broken in one step: a harness that silently does nothing reports a clean pass, and the author's own tests do not test the author. The guard now asserts the LAYOUT MODE and the child ORDER, because those are the facts that were silently wrong, and every scripted edit asserts its anchor.
findings.closes_when: The page asserts it is a flex row with rail, stage and inspector in order, and no scripted edit can fail without raising.
